weeks.title: Sharing a proper fraction
weeks.objective: Divide a proper fraction into equal whole-number shares.

connection.before: Recall that fraction multiplication finds a part of a quantity and can check an equal share.
connection.after: Fraction fluency supports rational-number operations in secondary school.

Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.

explanation: Imagine a paper strip as one whole. Shade 3 of its 4 equal pieces and share the shaded length equally between 2 people. Splitting every quarter into two pieces makes eighths; each person receives 3 eighths. The unshaded part is not part of the amount being shared.

The bar records (3/4) ÷ 2 = 3/8. Dividing a fraction by a whole number multiplies the denominator by that number because each original piece is subdivided. You may instead divide the numerator first when it is divisible, as (6/7) ÷ 3 = 2/7.

An equal share must be smaller than the starting amount when more than one recipient shares it. Do not divide both numerator and denominator by the number of recipients: that would preserve the original fraction. Multiply one share by the number of recipients to check the starting amount.

examples.prompt: Share 3/4 m of ribbon equally between 2 cards. How much ribbon goes on each card?
steps: Shade three quarters of a whole strip. Split each quarter in half to make six shaded eighths, then allocate half of those pieces to each card.
Simplify to 3/8; multiplying this by 2 returns 3/4.

examples.prompt: A jug contains 5/6 L. It is shared equally between 5 cups. Find the amount in one cup.
steps: Mark the jug as five equal sixth-litre pieces. Sharing among five cups assigns one of those pieces to each cup.
Simplify to 1/6; multiplying this by 5 returns 5/6.

items.prompt: Three children share 3/8 kg of clay equally. Find each share.
steps: Simplify to 1/8; multiplying this by 3 returns 3/8.

items.prompt: A 7/10 bar is shared between 7 people. How many twentieths does each receive?
steps: Each share is (7/10) ÷ 7 = 1/10.
Rename 1/10 as 2/20; seven shares total 14/20 = 7/10.

items.prompt: Which is larger: (2/5) ÷ 2 or (2/5) ÷ 4? Explain.
steps: The shares are 1/5 and 1/10 respectively.
Sharing the same amount between fewer people gives a larger share.

items.prompt: A learner writes (6/7) ÷ 3 = 2/7. Explain this using seven equal strip pieces.
items.answer: Share the six shaded sevenths into three groups of two sevenths.
steps: The denominator 7 describes each piece.
Each group has 2 pieces, and 3 × 2/7 = 6/7.

steps: Divide the three fifth-pieces among three groups: one fifth per group.

items.prompt: Two equal shares together contain 5/12 L. State the division and each share.
steps: Split each twelfth into two equal parts.
Each share contains five twenty-fourths; doubling gives 10/24 = 5/12.

items.prompt: What original fraction was shared if 4 people each received 2/15 of a whole cake?
steps: Recombine four equal shares: 4 × 2/15.

items.prompt: A 3/10 kg packet is divided into 3 equal bags. Two bags are used. How much remains?

items.prompt: Can three equal shares of 5/6 L each be 5/12 L? Explain.
items.answer: No; each share should be 5/18 L.

items.prompt: A painter shares 2/9 L equally among 6 trays. Find the amount per tray.
steps: Simplify to 1/27; multiplying this by 6 returns 2/9.

items.prompt: A strip of length 4/5 m is halved, then one half is halved again. Find the smaller piece.
steps: First half: (4/5) ÷ 2 = 2/5 m.
Halve 2/5 again to obtain 1/5 m; four such pieces make 4/5 m.

items.prompt: Give two different proper fractions which, when each is divided by 2, give a result below 1/4.
steps: Their halves are 1/6 and 1/5, both below 1/4.
Any two distinct positive proper fractions below 1/2 work; check by halving each.

weeks.title: Counting fractional groups
weeks.objective: Interpret whole-number division by a proper fraction as counting groups.

connection.before: Divide a proper fraction into equal whole-number shares.
connection.after: Fraction fluency supports rational-number operations in secondary school.

days: Build or sketch a model for counting fractional groups; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: Place four whole strips end to end and mark halves. Eight half-strip groups fit, so 4 ÷ (1/2) = 8. A quotient can exceed the dividend because the unit being counted is smaller than one whole. Say the group size aloud before choosing an operation.

For 3 ÷ (2/5), rename the three wholes as 15 fifths. Each group needs 2 fifths, so the number of groups is 15 ÷ 2 = 15/2. The final half-group contains 1 fifth, which is half of a 2-fifths group; it is not half a whole.

A measurement quotient can include part of a group. If the question asks for complete containers, count only whole groups and describe the leftover separately. Multiplying the number of groups, including any fractional group, by the group size checks the total amount.

examples.prompt: How many 3/4 L portions are in 6 L?
steps: Rename the six litres as 24 quarter-litres. Each portion must collect three of those quarter-litres.
Simplify to 8; multiplying this by 3/4 returns 6.

examples.prompt: A 2 m strip is measured in lengths of 3/5 m. How many such lengths does it contain, allowing a fractional length?
steps: Rename the two-metre strip as ten fifth-metres. Each measuring length is a group of three fifth-metres.
Simplify to 10/3; multiplying this by 3/5 returns 2.

weeks.title: One fraction measured by another
weeks.objective: Divide a proper fraction by a proper fraction using common pieces.

connection.before: Interpret whole-number division by a proper fraction as counting groups.
connection.after: Fraction fluency supports rational-number operations in secondary school.

days: Build or sketch a model for one fraction measured by another; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: A 3/4 strip contains three quarter-pieces. If the measuring piece is 1/8 of a whole, subdivide each quarter into two eighths. The shaded amount contains six eighths, so (3/4) ÷ (1/8) = 6. Both fractions must refer to the same whole.

If a 2/3 strip is measured with 3/4 strips, rename both amounts in twelfths: 8/12 ÷ 9/12. Eight small pieces divided by nine small pieces per group gives 8/9 of a group. The common denominator disappears because both amounts are counted in identical pieces.

The symbolic shortcut multiplies the first fraction by the reciprocal of the second. Reverse only the divisor. Compare the two amounts first: if the dividend is smaller than the divisor, fewer than one group fits. Check the quotient by multiplying it by the original divisor.

examples.prompt: How many 1/6 L portions fit into 3/4 L?
steps: Use twelfths of a litre: 3/4 L is nine twelfths and 1/6 L is two twelfths. The question counts two-piece groups within nine pieces.
Simplify to 9/2; multiplying this by 1/6 returns 3/4.

examples.prompt: What fraction of a 4/5 m ribbon is a 2/3 m ribbon?
steps: Use fifteenths of a metre: the shorter ribbon is ten fifteenths while the reference ribbon is twelve fifteenths. Compare ten pieces with a twelve-piece group.
Simplify to 5/6; multiplying this by 4/5 returns 2/3.

weeks.title: Choose the fraction division model
weeks.objective: Distinguish equal shares, group counts and remaining amounts in fraction problems.

connection.before: Divide a proper fraction by a proper fraction using common pieces.
connection.after: Fraction fluency supports rational-number operations in secondary school.

days: Build or sketch a model for choose the fraction division model; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: The same numbers can describe different questions. Sharing 2/3 L between four cups asks for litres per cup. Measuring 2/3 L with a 1/4 L scoop asks for scoopfuls. Label the unknown before writing a division so the quotient has a sensible unit.

Use a bar to separate operations in a two-step problem. If part of a supply is used first, mark the used section and divide only the remainder. If equal portions are made first, find one portion before deciding how much several portions use. Keep the original whole consistent throughout.

Interpret fractional answers in context. A quotient of 7/2 scoopfuls means three complete scoopfuls plus half a scoopful; the leftover volume is found using the scoop size. A multiplication check restores the amount divided, and adding any earlier used amount restores the original supply.

examples.prompt: A jug holds 5/6 L. After 1/3 L is used, the rest is shared equally between 3 cups. Find each share.
steps: Show the initial jug as five sixth-litre pieces. The used third removes two of those pieces, leaving three pieces to share.
The remaining bar is 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2 L.

examples.prompt: A 3/4 m strip makes 1/5 m pieces. Find the complete-piece count and leftover length.
steps: Mark the strip in twentieths: the supply is fifteen twentieths and a full piece needs four twentieths. Three groups fit, with a partial group remaining.
Three pieces use 3/5 = 12/20 m from the available 15/20 m.
The remainder is 3/20 m, less than the 4/20 m needed for another piece.

worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Share 7/9 kg equally among 7 bowls. Find the mass per bowl.
steps: Simplify to 1/9; multiplying this by 7 returns 7/9.

items.prompt: Count 2/7 L portions in 6/7 L.
steps: Simplify to 3; multiplying this by 2/7 returns 6/7.

items.prompt: Choose an operation for: 3/5 m is cut into five equal lengths. Then solve.
steps: The number of recipients is five, so this is equal sharing.
Five lengths of 3/25 m recombine to 15/25 = 3/5 m.

items.prompt: Choose an operation for: each badge needs 1/6 m tape and there is 2/3 m. Then solve.
steps: The unknown counts groups of size 1/6 m.
Four sixths make 2/3 m, so exactly four badges can be made.

items.prompt: A 4/5 L drink is split into 4 equal cups. How much is in 3 of the cups?
steps: Each cup holds (4/5) ÷ 4 = 1/5 L.
Three cups hold 3 × 1/5 = 3/5 L.

items.prompt: Explain why 1/2 ÷ 3 and 1/2 ÷ 1/3 answer different questions.
items.answer: They give 1/6 per share and 3/2 third-sized groups.
steps: The first divides a half among three recipients.
The second asks how many one-third units fit into a half; the divisor is a size.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Choose the fraction division model
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A packet contains 7/8 kg. Use 1/8 kg, then make 1/4 kg bags. How many bags?
steps: The remainder is 6/8 = 3/4 kg.
(3/4) ÷ (1/4) = 3; used amount plus bags is 1/8 + 3/4 = 7/8.

items.prompt: Five equal jars together hold 2/3 L. A sixth identical jar is filled to the same level. What do all six hold?
steps: Each jar contains (2/3) ÷ 5 = 2/15 L.
Six jars contain 12/15 = 4/5 L.

items.prompt: A learner divides 5/6 by 1/4 and reports 10/3 L. What should the unit be if 1/4 L is one cupful?
steps: Litres divided by litres per cupful counts cupfuls.
The quotient is 5/6 × 4 = 10/3; it is a count measured in cupfuls.

items.prompt: A 2/5 m ribbon is one third of a longer ribbon. Find the longer length.
steps: Three equal 2/5 m bars make the whole ribbon.
3 × 2/5 = 6/5 m; dividing this by three returns the known part.

items.prompt: A 5/7 kg clay block is divided into 5/14 kg blocks. How many blocks?
steps: Simplify to 2; multiplying this by 5/14 returns 5/7.

items.prompt: A recipe needs 2/3 L of milk. What fraction of one recipe can 1/2 L make?
steps: Compare available milk with milk per recipe: (1/2) ÷ (2/3).
The quotient is 3/4; 3/4 × 2/3 = 1/2 L.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Choose the fraction division model
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A 9/10 L bottle fills 1/4 L cups. Is four full cups possible? Explain.
items.answer: No; only 3 full cups, with 3/20 L left.
steps: Four cups require 1 L, more than 9/10 L.
Three use 3/4 L; 9/10 − 3/4 = 3/20 L remains.

items.prompt: After 2 of 6 equal portions are removed from 3/4 kg of dough, how much remains?
steps: One portion is (3/4) ÷ 6 = 1/8 kg.
Four portions remain, totalling 4/8 = 1/2 kg.

items.prompt: A 5/8 m strip and a 3/8 m strip are joined without overlap. How many 1/4 m lengths are in the joined strip?
steps: The joined length is 5/8 + 3/8 = 1 m.
1 ÷ (1/4) = 4; the joined strip contains four quarters.

items.prompt: A learner says (2/3) ÷ (4/5) = 5/6 means 5/6 L always. Explain when the unit would instead be a batch.
items.answer: When 2/3 L is available and each batch needs 4/5 L.
steps: The quotient compares litres available with litres needed per batch.
It therefore counts 5/6 of a batch; multiplication by 4/5 L per batch recovers 2/3 L.

items.prompt: Find a missing starting mass: after 1/6 kg is used, 3 portions of 2/9 kg remain.
steps: The remaining portions total 3 × 2/9 = 2/3 kg.
Add the used amount: 2/3 + 1/6 = 5/6 kg.

items.prompt: Invent a valid equal-sharing story with quotient 1/12 kg and four recipients. State the total.
items.answer: Example: share 1/3 kg of rice among four people.
steps: Four shares of 1/12 kg total 4/12 = 1/3 kg.
The story must divide this total equally into four shares; other matching contexts are valid.

weeks.title: Read and simplify ratios
weeks.objective: Compare two quantities in the stated order using a common unit.

connection.before: Distinguish equal shares, group counts and remaining amounts in fraction problems.
connection.after: S1 extends ratios to fractional and decimal quantities.

days: Build or sketch a model for read and simplify ratios; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: A row of 6 red counters and 9 blue counters can be regrouped into 3 identical sets, each containing 2 red and 3 blue. The red-to-blue ratio is 6:9 = 2:3. A ratio compares quantities in a stated order; reversing the labels reverses the terms.

Equivalent ratios describe the same multiplicative comparison. Multiply or divide every term by the same positive number. A bar with two equal units for red and three for blue represents 2:3, but a ratio alone does not tell us the physical size of one unit.

Part-to-part and part-to-whole comparisons answer different questions. With 2 red units and 3 blue units, the whole is 5 units, so the red fraction is 2/5, not 2/3. First match units such as centimetres before comparing measured lengths.

examples.prompt: There are 8 red beads and 12 blue beads. Simplify the red:blue ratio.
steps: Find a common grouping size for 8 red and 12 blue beads: both can be grouped in sets of 4.
There are 8 ÷ 4 = 2 red groups and 12 ÷ 4 = 3 blue groups, giving the ratio 2:3.
Check by rebuilding: four copies of 2 red and 3 blue give the original 8 red and 12 blue; the order matches the labels.

examples.prompt: Green:yellow counters = 3:5. What fraction of all counters is yellow?
steps: Draw three equal green units and five equal yellow units. The fraction denominator must count both colours together.
The whole bar has 3 + 5 = 8 equal units.
Yellow occupies five of those eight units, giving 5/8.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Read and simplify ratios
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Simplify cats:dogs when there are 10 cats and 15 dogs.
steps: Group each quantity in sets of 5.
Divide every term by 5: 10:15 = 2:3; the order stays unchanged.

items.prompt: Write the simplest pencil:pen ratio for 18 pencils and 24 pens.
steps: Group each quantity in sets of 6.
Divide every term by 6: 18:24 = 3:4; the order stays unchanged.

items.prompt: A design uses 14 white tiles and 21 black tiles. Simplify white:black.
steps: Group each quantity in sets of 7.
Divide every term by 7: 14:21 = 2:3; the order stays unchanged.

items.prompt: Blue:red = 4:7. Write red:blue.
steps: The requested order begins with red.
Red has seven units and blue has four; reverse both labels and terms.

items.prompt: Orange:purple = 2:5. What fraction is orange?
steps: The two parts together contain seven equal units.
Orange occupies two units, so its fraction is 2/7.

items.prompt: Is 6:10 equivalent to 9:15? Explain.
steps: Divide the first ratio by 2 and the second by 3.
Both comparisons use three first-part units for every five second-part units.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Read and simplify ratios
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Compare lengths A = 120 cm and B = 80 cm as A:B in simplest form.
steps: Group each quantity in sets of 40.
Divide every term by 40: 120:80 = 3:2; the order stays unchanged.

items.prompt: Length P is 2 m and length Q is 50 cm. Find P:Q.
steps: Convert 2 m to 200 cm so both terms measure the same unit.
200:50 simplifies by dividing each term by 50.

items.prompt: Complete 3:8 = 12:___ and explain.
steps: The first term was multiplied by 4.
Multiply the second term by the same factor: 8 × 4 = 32.

items.prompt: A learner turns 4:6 into 5:7 by adding 1 to each term. Is it equivalent?
steps: 4:6 simplifies to 2:3, but 5:7 does not.
Equivalent ratios scale both terms; for example doubling 4:6 gives 8:12.

items.prompt: A basket has apples:pears = 5:2. Write apples:all fruit.
steps: All fruit includes 5 + 2 = 7 equal units.
Compare the five apple units with all seven units.

items.prompt: Does the ratio boys:girls = 3:4 prove there are 7 children? Explain.
steps: The ratio tells us there are seven equal units in total.
Each unit could contain one or more children, so the total is not fixed.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Read and simplify ratios
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A mixture uses 45 g of seeds and 30 g of oats. Simplify seeds:oats.
steps: Group each quantity in sets of 15.
Divide every term by 15: 45:30 = 3:2; the order stays unchanged.

items.prompt: Two drawings show red:blue counts of 4:9 and 8:18. Which has a larger red fraction?
steps: Doubling both counts preserves the ratio.
The red fractions are 4/13 and 8/26 = 4/13.

items.prompt: In a row of 16 beads, 6 are yellow and the rest are green. Find yellow:green in simplest form.
steps: Green beads = 16 − 6 = 10.
Yellow:green = 6:10 = 3:5.

items.prompt: A class has 12 left-handed and 20 right-handed pupils. Write right-handed:all pupils in simplest form.
steps: The total is 12 + 20 = 32.
The requested ratio is 20:32; divide by 4 to get 5:8.

items.prompt: Supply two different whole-number pairs with ratio 7:3.
steps: Multiply both terms of 7:3 by one common positive whole number per pair.
The pairs must simplify to 7:3; many other choices work.

items.prompt: A rope has two parts in ratio 1:4. A learner says the shorter part is 1/4 of the whole. Correct this.
items.answer: The shorter part is 1/5 of the whole.
steps: The whole consists of 1 + 4 = 5 units.
One quarter compares the shorter part to the longer part; one fifth compares it to the whole.

weeks.title: Share a total in a two-part ratio
weeks.objective: Use the sum of ratio units to divide a known total.

connection.before: Compare two quantities in the stated order using a common unit.
connection.after: S1 extends ratios to fractional and decimal quantities.

days: Build or sketch a model for share a total in a two-part ratio; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: To divide 40 counters in the ratio 3:5, draw one bar of three units and another of five equally sized units. Together the eight units represent all 40 counters. One unit is 40 ÷ 8 = 5 counters, so the two shares are 15 and 25.

The total belongs to the sum of the ratio terms, not to either term by itself. The symbolic sequence is total ÷ sum of terms, followed by multiplication by the required term. Fractions give the same result: the first share is 3/8 of the total.

Check both the sum and the comparison. Shares that add to the total can still have the wrong ratio. For indivisible objects, a stated exact whole-number ratio and total must produce whole-number shares; a fractional pupil or tile indicates incompatible conditions.

examples.prompt: Share 56 stickers in the ratio A:B = 3:4. How many does B receive?
steps: Draw A with three equal units and B with four; bracket both bars together and label their total 56 stickers.
The bar contains 7 equal units, so one unit is 56 ÷ 7 = 8.
The requested 4 units give 32; all parts together recover 56.

examples.prompt: A 72 cm cord has short:long parts = 2:7. Find the short length.
steps: Draw a two-unit short piece and a seven-unit long piece on the same cord; together they occupy all 72 cm.
The bar contains 9 equal units, so one unit is 72 ÷ 9 = 8.
The requested 2 units give 16; all parts together recover 72.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Share a total in a two-part ratio
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Divide 45 counters in red:blue = 2:3. Find red.
steps: The bar contains 5 equal units, so one unit is 45 ÷ 5 = 9.
The requested 2 units give 18; all parts together recover 45.

items.prompt: A $96 fund is shared in a 5:7 ratio. Find the larger share.
steps: The bar contains 12 equal units, so one unit is 96 ÷ 12 = 8.
The requested 7 units give 56; all parts together recover 96.

items.prompt: Share 84 seeds as oak:pine = 4:3. Find pine.
steps: The bar contains 7 equal units, so one unit is 84 ÷ 7 = 12.
The requested 3 units give 36; all parts together recover 84.

items.prompt: Forty-eight books are split fiction:nonfiction = 5:3. How many units are there and how large is one unit?
steps: Add the ratio terms: 5 + 3 = 8.
The total 48 books occupies eight units, so divide 48 by 8.

items.prompt: A bar has 2 units for A and 9 for B, totalling 77 marbles. Find both shares.
steps: One unit is 77 ÷ 11 = 7 marbles.
Multiply by 2 and 9; 14 + 63 = 77 and 14:63 = 2:9.

items.prompt: A learner splits 60 in ratio 1:4 as 15 and 45. Correct the split.
steps: The total represents five units, so one unit is 12.
The shares 12 and 48 are in ratio 1:4; 15:45 would be 1:3.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Share a total in a two-part ratio
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A garden has 108 flowers in red:white = 7:5. Find red flowers.
steps: The bar contains 12 equal units, so one unit is 108 ÷ 12 = 9.
The requested 7 units give 63; all parts together recover 108.

items.prompt: Two shelves hold 70 books in a 3:2 ratio. Find the smaller count.
steps: The bar contains 5 equal units, so one unit is 70 ÷ 5 = 14.
The requested 2 units give 28; all parts together recover 70.

items.prompt: Split 64 kg of grain into rice:millet = 3:5. Give both masses.
steps: One of eight ratio units is 64 ÷ 8 = 8 kg.
Three units weigh 24 kg and five weigh 40 kg; their sum is 64 kg.

items.prompt: Can 25 identical tokens be shared exactly in ratio 2:4 without breaking tokens?
steps: The simplest ratio is 1:2, so the total must be divisible by 3.
25 is not a multiple of 3; exact whole-token shares are impossible.

items.prompt: Two parts of a 99 cm ribbon have ratio 4:7. How much longer is the longer part?
steps: One unit is 99 ÷ 11 = 9 cm.
The difference is 7 − 4 = 3 units, or 27 cm.

items.prompt: An 80-item collection has A:B = 3:5. Find the fraction and number belonging to A.
steps: The whole has eight ratio units, of which A occupies three.
3/8 × 80 = 30; B then has 50 and the ratio is 3:5.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Share a total in a two-part ratio
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A 132 L mixture has juice:water = 5:6. Find the juice volume.
steps: The bar contains 11 equal units, so one unit is 132 ÷ 11 = 12.
The requested 5 units give 60; all parts together recover 132.

items.prompt: A 90 cm strip is split 4:5. If the shorter piece is then halved, what is each half?
steps: The shorter piece is 4/9 × 90 = 40 cm.
Halve 40 cm to obtain 20 cm; preserve the original ratio before cutting.

items.prompt: A and B share $110 in ratio 6:5. B spends $14. How much does B have left?
steps: One unit is 110 ÷ 11 = $10, so B receives $50.
Subtract the spending: 50 − 14 = $36.

items.prompt: Two teams share 78 balls in ratio 5:8. A proposed split is 30 and 48. Verify it fully.
steps: 30 + 48 = 78, so the total is preserved.
30:48 simplifies to 5:8 by dividing both terms by 6.

items.prompt: Find a total below 50 that can be shared as whole objects in ratio 3:7, with both shares greater than 5.
steps: The total must be a multiple of ten.
20 works because 3 × 2 = 6 and 7 × 2 = 14; 30 and 40 also work.

items.prompt: A 36 L mixture has red:blue liquid = 4:5. Another 4 L of red is added. Find the new volumes, without simplifying a new ratio.
steps: Originally one unit is 4 L, giving 16 L red and 20 L blue.
Only red changes: 16 + 4 = 20 L; the new total is 40 L.

weeks.title: Recover ratio amounts from one part
weeks.objective: Find a common ratio unit when one part or the difference is known.

connection.before: Use the sum of ratio units to divide a known total.
connection.after: S1 extends ratios to fractional and decimal quantities.

days: Build or sketch a model for recover ratio amounts from one part; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: If A:B = 3:7 and A is 18, the three-unit bar represents 18, so one unit is 6. B has seven of the same units and equals 42. Do not divide 18 by the total of ten units, because 18 labels only A.

A difference can also label a section of a bar. If the longer bar has seven units and the shorter has three, the excess is four units. A known difference of 28 therefore gives one unit as 28 ÷ 4 = 7. Once the unit is known, either part and the total follow.

Mark the known number at the correct location: one bar, both bars together, or the excess. The division must match that label. Check a difference problem by subtracting the final parts, then separately verify the ratio.

examples.prompt: A:B = 4:9. A has 28 cards. How many cards does B have?
steps: Label only the four-unit A bar with 28 cards. Extend an equal-unit bar to nine units for B.
The known 4 units represent 28, so one unit is 28 ÷ 4 = 7.
The requested 9 units give 63; the other part is 63.

examples.prompt: Two lengths have ratio 2:5 and differ by 24 cm. Find both lengths.
steps: Align the two-unit and five-unit bars at their left ends. The three-unit overhang, rather than the whole long bar, is the 24 cm difference.
The excess is 5 − 2 = 3 units, so one unit is 24 ÷ 3 = 8 cm.
The lengths are 2 × 8 and 5 × 8; their difference is 24 cm.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Recover ratio amounts from one part
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Red:blue = 3:8. There are 21 red beads. Find blue.
steps: The known 3 units represent 21, so one unit is 21 ÷ 3 = 7.
The requested 8 units give 56; the other part is 56.

items.prompt: A:B = 5:6. A weighs 35 kg. Find the total mass.
steps: The known 5 units represent 35, so one unit is 35 ÷ 5 = 7.
The requested 11 units give 77; the other part is 42.

items.prompt: Small:large = 2:7. There are 18 small boxes. Find large boxes.
steps: The known 2 units represent 18, so one unit is 18 ÷ 2 = 9.
The requested 7 units give 63; the other part is 63.

items.prompt: Boys:girls = 4:5 and there are 35 girls. Find boys.
steps: The known count labels five units, so one unit is 35 ÷ 5 = 7.
Four units contain 28 boys; 28:35 = 4:5.

items.prompt: A:B = 6:11. B exceeds A by 30. Find one unit.
steps: The excess is five units.
30 ÷ 5 = 6; the actual parts would be 36 and 66.

items.prompt: A:B = 3:4 and A = 24. A learner divides 24 by 7. Why is this wrong?
items.answer: 24 labels three units, so one unit is 8.
steps: Seven units label the combined total, which is unknown.
B is 32 and the total is 56; dividing 56 by 7 would be valid.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Recover ratio amounts from one part
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: P:Q = 7:3. P has 56 stamps. Find Q.
steps: The known 7 units represent 56, so one unit is 56 ÷ 7 = 8.
The requested 3 units give 24; the other part is 24.

items.prompt: Water:juice = 9:2. Water is 63 L. Find the whole mixture.
steps: The known 9 units represent 63, so one unit is 63 ÷ 9 = 7.
The requested 11 units give 77; the other part is 14.

items.prompt: Two amounts in ratio 5:8 differ by $27. Find the smaller amount.
steps: The difference is three units, so one unit is $9.
Five units give $45; the other amount $72 is $27 greater.

items.prompt: Two teams have members in ratio 3:5. The larger team has 12 more people. Find the total.
steps: Two excess units represent 12 people, so one unit is 6.
Eight total units represent 48 people; the teams have 18 and 30.

items.prompt: A:B = 1:6. The difference is 35. Find B.
steps: The difference is five units, making one unit 7.
B has six units, or 42; A is 7 and 42 − 7 = 35.

items.prompt: A:B = 2:3. A = 14 and B = 24 are proposed. Identify which condition fails.
steps: A implies one unit is 14 ÷ 2 = 7.
B would need to be 3 × 7 = 21; 14:24 is 7:12.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Recover ratio amounts from one part
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A 4:7 mixture contains 32 g of its first ingredient. Find the second ingredient and total.
steps: Four units weigh 32 g, so one unit weighs 8 g.
Seven units weigh 56 g, and 32 + 56 = 88 g.

items.prompt: A:B = 5:9. B has 36 more tokens. A gives away 5 tokens. How many does A keep?
steps: Four excess units represent 36, so one unit is 9 and A starts with 45.
Subtract 5 from A only: 45 − 5 = 40.

items.prompt: A:B = 3:10. A has 27 bottles. B packs its bottles into boxes of 6. How many boxes?
steps: One unit is 9 bottles, so B has 90.
90 ÷ 6 = 15 full boxes.

items.prompt: Lengths P:Q = 8:5. P is 21 cm longer. Find Q and check the difference.
steps: Three excess units make 21 cm, so one unit is 7 cm.

items.prompt: Can whole-number counts in ratio 4:9 differ by 18? Explain.
steps: The difference must be five ratio units.
18 ÷ 5 = 3.6 would make counts 14.4 and 32.4, which are not whole objects.

items.prompt: Construct two whole-number amounts in ratio 2:5 whose difference exceeds 20.
steps: Choose a unit greater than 20 ÷ 3; a unit of 8 works.
Then the parts are 16 and 40 and the difference is 24; many larger units work.

weeks.title: Three-part ratio bars
weeks.objective: Allocate and compare three quantities using shared equal units.

connection.before: Find a common ratio unit when one part or the difference is known.
connection.after: S1 extends ratios to fractional and decimal quantities.

days: Build or sketch a model for three-part ratio bars; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: A three-part ratio A:B:C = 2:3:5 uses a single common unit for all three bars. If the total is 80, the ten units make one unit worth 8, and the parts are 16, 24 and 40. The same scale factor must apply to every term.

Simplification also acts on all three terms. The ratio 12:18:30 can be divided by 6 to become 2:3:5. Dividing only two terms changes the comparison. A pair within the triple can be compared separately, but its total is not the total of all three bars.

When one part is given, use its term to find the unit. When two parts are combined, add only their terms. A check must include all three quantities: their sum should equal the total and each quantity divided by its ratio term should give the same unit.

examples.prompt: Share 90 counters among A:B:C = 2:3:4. Find C.
steps: Draw bars of two, three and four equal units, all using the same unit length; their combined total is 90 counters.
The bar contains 9 equal units, so one unit is 90 ÷ 9 = 10.
The requested 4 units give 40; all parts together recover 90.

examples.prompt: Simplify the three-part ratio 18:24:42.
steps: A grouping size of 6 divides all three quantities 18, 24 and 42.
Divide every term by 6 to obtain 3:4:7; the common group size stays the same for all three.
Rebuild the quantities: 3 × 6 = 18, 4 × 6 = 24 and 7 × 6 = 42, confirming all three comparisons.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Three-part ratio bars
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A:B:C = 1:2:5 with total 64. Find B.
steps: The bar contains 8 equal units, so one unit is 64 ÷ 8 = 8.
The requested 2 units give 16; all parts together recover 64.

items.prompt: Divide 120 g in the ratio 3:4:5. Find the first mass.
steps: The bar contains 12 equal units, so one unit is 120 ÷ 12 = 10.
The requested 3 units give 30; all parts together recover 120.

items.prompt: Simplify red:green:blue = 15:25:35.
steps: Group each quantity in sets of 5.
Divide every term by 5: 15:25:35 = 3:5:7; the order stays unchanged.

items.prompt: A:B:C = 4:2:3. What fraction of the total is C?
steps: The total is nine equal units.
C has three units, so 3/9 = 1/3.

items.prompt: Three bars have 2, 5 and 7 units. Together they represent 98 L. Find all three volumes.
steps: The fourteen units give one unit as 98 ÷ 14 = 7 L.
Multiply 7 L by 2, 5 and 7; the volumes sum to 98 L.

items.prompt: A learner simplifies 6:9:12 to 2:3:12. Correct it.
steps: The first two terms were divided by 3.
The third term must also be divided by 3 to preserve the common unit.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Three-part ratio bars
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Three teams share 144 cards in ratio 5:4:3. Find the smallest share.
steps: The bar contains 12 equal units, so one unit is 144 ÷ 12 = 12.
The requested 3 units give 36; all parts together recover 144.

items.prompt: A:B:C = 2:6:7 and B = 42. Find A and C.
steps: Six units equal 42, so one unit is 7.
Two units equal 14 and seven units equal 49.

items.prompt: Red:blue:yellow = 3:5:2. Red and yellow together number 40. Find blue.
steps: Red and yellow together occupy 3 + 2 = 5 units.
One unit is 8, so blue also has 5 × 8 = 40.

items.prompt: A:B:C = 3:4:8. C exceeds A by 25. Find the total.
steps: The excess is 8 − 3 = 5 units, so one unit is 5.
The fifteen total units give 15 × 5 = 75.

items.prompt: For A:B:C = 4:6:9, write A:B in simplest form.
steps: Use the first two terms in their original order: 4:6.
Divide both by 2; C is not part of this pairwise comparison.

items.prompt: For P:Q:R = 1:3:4, what fraction of P and Q combined is Q?
steps: Only P and Q belong to the requested whole, giving four units.
Q occupies three of these units; do not use all eight units.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Three-part ratio bars
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A $180 budget is divided supplies:food:prizes = 4:3:2. Find food money.
steps: The bar contains 9 equal units, so one unit is 180 ÷ 9 = 20.
The requested 3 units give 60; all parts together recover 180.

items.prompt: A:B:C = 2:3:6 with total 88. C gives 8 to A. Find the new counts.
steps: One unit is 8, so the starting counts are 16, 24 and 48.
Transfer 8: add it to A and subtract it from C; the total stays 88.

items.prompt: Can 40 marbles be split exactly in ratio 2:3:4?
steps: There are nine common units in all.
40 ÷ 9 is not a whole number, so the first share 80/9 would not be a whole count.

items.prompt: In a 5:2:3 mixture totalling 70 kg, the second ingredient costs $4 per kg. Find its cost.
steps: The second ingredient is 2/10 × 70 = 14 kg.
At $4 per kg its cost is 14 × 4 = $56.

items.prompt: Three proposed shares are 24, 36 and 60. Verify that they fit ratio 2:3:5 and total 120.
steps: 24 ÷ 2 = 36 ÷ 3 = 60 ÷ 5 = 12, the common unit.
24 + 36 + 60 = 120 verifies the total.

items.prompt: Give a three-part ratio for which the middle part is half the whole. Explain your choice.
steps: The first and third terms together must equal the middle term.
Here the whole has ten units and the middle has five; other positive whole-number examples work.

weeks.title: Ratio changes and unchanged quantities
weeks.objective: Track what stays fixed when ratio quantities change.

connection.before: Allocate and compare three quantities using shared equal units.
connection.after: S1 extends ratios to fractional and decimal quantities.

days: Build or sketch a model for ratio changes and unchanged quantities; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: When objects move from one group to another, the total stays fixed but both parts change. Start with a bar model of the original ratio and total. Apply the transfer to the actual counts, then compare the new counts; ratio terms are not automatically object counts.

When objects are added from outside, the untouched group stays fixed and the total grows. If red:blue is 2:3 with 12 blue, red is 8. Adding 4 red makes 12:12 = 1:1. The original one-unit size of 4 helped find counts but does not force the new ratio to have the same term sum.

For comparison problems, keep the reference whole clear. A larger first term alone does not prove a larger proportion. Compare part-to-whole fractions or scale to a shared second part. Always check whether a described change preserves the total, one part, or neither.

examples.prompt: A:B = 3:5 and there are 64 counters. B gives 8 to A. Find the new ratio.
steps: The initial ratio has eight total units. A transfer moves counters between bars while keeping the full 64-counter total fixed.
One unit is 8, so the original counts are 24 and 40.
After transfer the counts are 32 and 32; simplify to 1:1.

examples.prompt: Red:blue = 2:7 with 28 blue beads. Add 12 red beads. Find the new ratio.
steps: Blue is the unchanged bar of seven units, labelled 28 beads. The added twelve beads extend only the red bar.
The old red count is 2 × (28 ÷ 7) = 8.
Red becomes 20 while blue stays 28; 20:28 = 5:7.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Ratio changes and unchanged quantities
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A:B = 1:3 with total 48. A receives 8 new objects. Find the new counts.
steps: Originally one unit is 12, so A = 12 and B = 36.
Only A grows by 8; the new total is 56.

items.prompt: A:B = 5:4 with total 81. A gives 9 to B. Find the new ratio.
steps: The starting counts are 45 and 36.
After transfer they are 36 and 45, which simplify to 4:5.

items.prompt: A recipe has seeds:oats = 3:7. Both amounts are doubled. What is the new ratio?
steps: Doubling gives the ratio 6:14.
Dividing both terms by 2 restores 3:7; the total mass doubles but the comparison stays the same.

items.prompt: A:B = 4:5. A is 20 and B is 25. Remove 5 from each. Find the new ratio.
steps: The remaining counts are 15 and 20.
Simplify 15:20 to 3:4; subtracting equal amounts does not preserve a ratio.

items.prompt: Which has the greater red fraction: red:blue = 2:3 or 3:7?
steps: The red fractions are 2/5 = 4/10 and 3/10.
Four tenths exceeds three tenths; compare against each whole.

items.prompt: A transfer changes counts from 18 and 30 to 22 and 26. How many moved, and in which direction?
items.answer: 4 moved from the second group to the first.
steps: The first group gained 22 − 18 = 4.
The second lost 30 − 26 = 4; the total stayed 48.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Ratio changes and unchanged quantities
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: P:Q = 7:2 and Q = 10. Add 15 to Q. Find P:Q afterward.
steps: One original unit is 5, so P = 35.
Q becomes 25; simplify 35:25 to 7:5.

items.prompt: A:B = 3:2 and A = 27. Remove 6 from A and 4 from B. Does the ratio stay the same?
steps: B starts at 18; the new counts are 21 and 14.
21:14 simplifies to 3:2 because a whole 3:2 batch was removed twice.

items.prompt: A:B:C = 2:3:5 with total 100. C gives 10 to A. Find the new simplest ratio.
steps: The initial counts are 20, 30 and 50.
After transfer they are 30, 30 and 40; divide by 10.

items.prompt: A:B = 2:5 with total 42. How many must B give A so that they are equal?
steps: The counts are 12 and 30, a difference of 18.
Each transferred object closes the gap by 2, so 18 ÷ 2 = 9.

items.prompt: A:B = 1:4 and A = 6. How many new objects must be added to A to make A:B = 1:2?
steps: B remains 24, so the target A is half of 24, or 12.
A must increase from 6 to 12, requiring 6 new objects.

items.prompt: A learner says adding 3 to counts 4 and 8 keeps ratio 1:2. Test the claim.
steps: The new counts are 7 and 11.
Double 7 is 14, not 11, so the old multiplicative comparison has changed.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Ratio changes and unchanged quantities
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A:B = 5:7 with total 96. A uses 8 objects and B uses 16. Find the remaining ratio.
steps: The initial counts are 40 and 56.
The remaining counts are 32 and 40, giving 4:5.

items.prompt: A mixture has juice:water = 2:3 and totals 25 L. Add 5 L water. Find the new juice fraction.
steps: Initially juice is 10 L and water is 15 L.
The new total is 30 L with juice unchanged at 10 L; 10/30 = 1/3.

items.prompt: A:B = 4:7 and A = 32. Both groups give away one quarter of their objects. Find the new counts and ratio.
steps: B starts with 56; each group retains 3/4 of its own count.
The retained counts are 24 and 42, and scaling both by 3/4 preserves 4:7.

items.prompt: Compare fruit mixtures apples:pears = 3:4 and 6:9. Which contains a greater apple fraction?
steps: The fractions are 3/7 and 6/15 = 2/5.
Use thirty-fifths: 15/35 is greater than 14/35.

items.prompt: Two groups start with 20 and 40 tokens. Find a positive transfer from the larger to the smaller that makes the new ratio 2:3.
steps: The total stays 60, so a 2:3 split needs 24 and 36.
The first must gain 4 while the second loses 4.

items.prompt: Explain why knowing an initial ratio 2:3 and that 4 objects are added to the first group does not determine a unique new ratio.
items.answer: The starting counts are not known.
steps: Starting from 2 and 3 gives 6:3 = 2:1.
Starting from 4 and 6 gives 8:6 = 4:3; both satisfy the initial ratio but produce different results.

weeks.title: Recover the percentage whole
weeks.objective: Find an unknown whole from a known percentage part.

connection.before: Track what stays fixed when ratio quantities change.
connection.after: S1 consolidates reverse percentages and distinguishes percentage points.

days: Build or sketch a model for recover the percentage whole; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.

explanation: A hundred-part bar makes the reference whole visible. If 25% is 18, one quarter of the bar is 18, so the full bar is four copies of 18, or 72. The given number is the percentage part, not automatically the whole.

explanation: An increase is the amount added to the original bar. A rise from 40 to 50 adds 10. Compare the extra 10 with the original 40: 10/40 = 25%. The final amount is therefore 125% of the original, not 25% of it.

To find a new amount, compute the stated percentage of the original and add it. To work backward, identify the final percentage first. After a 15% increase the final amount is 115%; if this is 69, the original is 69 ÷ 115 × 100 = 60.

The denominator in percentage change is the original amount. Comparing the increase with the final amount answers a different question. Use a bar with the original 100% section and an added section to keep the two wholes distinct; an increase should produce a larger positive amount.

examples.prompt: A club grows from 48 to 60 members. Find the percentage increase.
steps: Use a 48-member original bar and extend it to 60 members. The added section is 12 members, compared with the original bar.
The added fraction of the original is 12/48 = 1/4.
One quarter is 25%, so the increase is 25%; a quarter of 48 is 12 and 48 + 12 = 60 checks it.

explanation: A reduction from 80 to 60 removes 20 from the original bar. Since 20/80 = 1/4, the decrease is 25%. The remaining 60 is 75% of the original. Keep separate labels for the amount lost, the amount retained and the original whole.

To apply a decrease, calculate the stated percentage of the original and subtract it. To calculate the decrease percentage from two amounts, subtract first and divide the difference by the original. Either method can be checked by adding the removed amount to the remainder.

Percentage decreases cannot exceed 100% when the quantity is a nonnegative stock or price. A decrease of 100% leaves zero. Equal raw decreases can have very different percentages when the original amounts differ, so compare both the difference and its reference whole.

The removed fraction of the original is 18/90 = 1/5.
One fifth is 20%, so the decrease is 20%; removing 18 from 90 restores the stated 72.

explanation: Draw two bars in sequence rather than treating successive changes as one addition of percentages. Increasing 100 by 20% gives 120. Decreasing that new 120 by 20% removes 24, leaving 96. The second twenty percent uses a different whole.

Compare proposed offers using a common starting price and explicitly stated conditions. A fixed reduction in dollars is different from a percentage reduction. The fall is 10/50 = 20%; the same difference has different reference wholes.

items.prompt: Find a positive starting amount for which a 50% increase followed by a 20% decrease ends at 72.
steps: Reverse the final decrease: 72 ÷ 0.8 = 90.
Reverse the first increase: 90 ÷ 1.5 = 60; the forward calculation confirms both stages.

weeks.title: Letters label equal bars
weeks.objective: Write simple expressions that represent a quantity and distinguish expressions from equations.

connection.before: Apply each percentage to the amount present at that stage.
connection.after: S1 introduces signed coefficients, brackets, formulas and linear graphs.

days: Build or sketch a model for letters label equal bars; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: A letter can label an unknown amount that remains the same within a problem. If each packet holds n counters, three matching packet bars contain n + n + n, written 3n. The letter is a number label, not a unit or the name of an object.

Attach loose quantities to the bar. Three packets and five loose counters contain 3n + 5 counters. The expression describes the total for any allowed packet count n; it does not yet state a particular total. The equation 3n + 5 = 26 adds a condition that can determine n.

Order matters in subtraction. Seven fewer than n is n − 7, while n fewer than seven is 7 − n. Use a short numerical trial to check your translation and specify a sensible whole-number range when the situation counts objects. This week uses simple expressions without brackets.

examples.prompt: Each pouch contains x beads. Write the total in 4 pouches and 3 loose beads.
steps: Draw four matching bars and label each x beads; put three single bead units beside them.
Four equal bars of x beads make x + x + x + x = 4x.
Add the three loose beads after counting the four pouches.

examples.prompt: A ribbon is y cm long. Cut off 8 cm. Write the remaining length and a sensible condition on y.
steps: Label the full ribbon y cm and mark an 8 cm section at one end to be removed.
The full bar has length y; the removed section is 8 cm.
Subtract the removed section; at least 8 cm must be available.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Letters label equal bars
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Write an expression for 6 bags each holding n marbles.
steps: The six bags contribute six equal n-sized bars.
Repeated addition n + n + n + n + n + n is written 6n.

items.prompt: A box contains a cards and 9 more are added. Express the new count.
steps: Begin with the unknown count a.
Adding nine objects extends the bar by nine units.

items.prompt: Write an expression for 5 fewer than b.
steps: Start at the amount b.
Remove five; substituting b = 12 gives 7, which is five fewer than twelve.

items.prompt: A notebook costs $p. Write the cost of 7 notebooks.
steps: Seven equal price bars each have value p.
The total is p added seven times, written 7p.

items.prompt: Two equal strips have length t cm each. A third strip is 4 cm long. Express the total.
steps: The equal strips together contribute 2t cm.
The separate 4 cm strip adds four to that total.

items.prompt: Does 3m + 2 = 20 describe an expression or an equation? Explain.
steps: The equals sign states that two quantities have the same value.
3m + 2 alone is an expression; setting it equal to 20 imposes a condition.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Letters label equal bars
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A jug contains v L. It fills 3 identical cups of 2 L each. Express the water left.
steps: The cups remove 3 × 2 = 6 L.
Subtract that known amount from v; the original amount must be at least 6 L.

items.prompt: A child has k stickers and buys two sheets of 8 stickers. Express the new number.
steps: The purchase adds 2 × 8 = 16 stickers.
Combine the starting k with the sixteen new stickers.

items.prompt: Write an expression for one fifth of q.
steps: Partition a q-sized bar into five equal parts.
Each part is q divided by five, written q/5.

items.prompt: A learner translates 9 more than 2r as 9r + 2. Correct it.
steps: Twice r is represented by two r-sized bars, or 2r.
Nine more means add the fixed number 9, not nine copies of r.

items.prompt: Each crate holds h bottles. There are 3 crates, and 4 bottles break. Express the unbroken count.
steps: Three crates initially contain 3h bottles.
Subtract the four broken bottles; the result cannot be negative.

items.prompt: Give a story represented by 5s + 7, defining s.
items.answer: Example: five packets each contain s seeds, plus seven loose seeds.
steps: Each packet contributes s, so five packets contribute 5s.
The seven loose seeds give the added 7; matching original stories are valid.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Letters label equal bars
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A bus has n passengers. At a stop 6 leave and 10 enter. Write the new count in simplest form.
steps: Removing six and adding ten changes the count by four.
The expression is n − 6 + 10 = n + 4; the initial six departures must be possible.

items.prompt: A 30 cm strip loses x cm. Write the remaining length and allowed whole-number values of x.
steps: The unknown is the amount removed, so subtract it from 30.
A nonnegative removed length cannot exceed the full strip.

items.prompt: A club has 4 teams of a pupils and 2 adult helpers. Write an expression for all people.
steps: Pupils contribute four equal a-sized groups.
The two helpers are extra people, so add 2 after multiplying.

items.prompt: Is n + n + n the same as n^3? Explain using n = 2.
steps: For n = 2, the sum is 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.
n^3 multiplies 2 × 2 × 2 = 8; repeated addition and repeated multiplication differ.

items.prompt: A pencil costs c cents. Mei has 100 cents and buys 4 pencils. Express her change.
steps: The cost is four equal c-cent amounts, or 4c.
Subtract the purchase cost from 100; spending cannot exceed the money available.

items.prompt: Name the unknown and write an equation: three identical boxes and 5 loose balls contain 29 balls in all.
items.answer: Let x be balls per box; 3x + 5 = 29
steps: Three equal box bars represent 3x balls.
Adding five loose balls gives the known total 29, so an equals sign is required.

weeks.title: Combine like quantities
weeks.objective: Simplify simple linear expressions by collecting matching letter terms and numbers.

connection.before: Write simple expressions that represent a quantity and distinguish expressions from equations.
connection.after: S1 introduces signed coefficients, brackets, formulas and linear graphs.

days: Build or sketch a model for combine like quantities; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: Use equal bar segments to see why 3x + 2x = 5x. The letter labels the same-sized segment, and the coefficients count how many segments there are. Combining x-terms changes the number of segments, not the value represented by x.

Loose number units must be combined separately. In 4x + 7 + 2x + 3, the x-bars make 6x and the loose units make 10, so the result is 6x + 10. An x-bar cannot be combined with a loose unit as if their sizes were known to match.

Subtraction removes matching bars or units: 7y − 3y = 4y. The coefficient 1 is usually not written, so 5y − 4y = y. Keep operations visible while collecting terms, and test a proposed simplification by substituting a small value; a single failure disproves it.

examples.prompt: Simplify 4x + 3x + 8.
steps: Draw four x-bars and three more identical x-bars; represent the eight units with separate small fixed blocks.
Combine the four and three equal x-bars to make seven x-bars.
The eight loose units remain separate because their size is known to be one, not x.

examples.prompt: Simplify 9a + 6 − 4a + 2.
steps: Begin with nine a-bars and six fixed blocks; remove four a-bars and add two more fixed blocks.
Removing four a-bars from nine leaves five a-bars.
The loose units total 6 + 2 = 8, giving 5a + 8.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Combine like quantities
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Simplify 2n + 5n.
steps: Both terms count n-sized bars.
Add the coefficients 2 + 5 = 7 and keep the common label n.

items.prompt: Simplify 8p − 3p.
steps: Start with eight p-sized bars.
Remove three identical bars, leaving five.

items.prompt: Simplify a + a + a + 4.
steps: Three copies of a make 3a.
The four loose units are added separately.

items.prompt: Simplify 6t + 2 + t + 5.
steps: The letter terms give 6t + t = 7t.
The number terms give 2 + 5 = 7.

items.prompt: Simplify 10m − 4m − 2m.
steps: Remove four m-bars from ten to leave six.
Remove two more to leave four m-bars.

items.prompt: Explain why 3x + 5 cannot generally become 8x.
items.answer: The five units are not five x-bars.
steps: But 8x = 16; this counterexample shows the expressions differ.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Combine like quantities
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Simplify 5b + 9 + 2b − 4.
steps: Collect matching b-bars: 5b + 2b = 7b.
Collect fixed units: 9 − 4 = 5.

items.prompt: Simplify 12q − 5q + 3q.
steps: Twelve bars minus five leaves seven.
Adding three more gives ten q-bars.

items.prompt: Simplify 4r + 11 − 3r.
steps: Four r-bars minus three r-bars leaves one r-bar.
One times r is written r; the eleven units remain.

items.prompt: A learner simplifies 7y − 2y + 6 as 5y + 6. Verify using y = 4.
steps: The original gives 28 − 8 + 6 = 26.
The simplified form gives 20 + 6 = 26; the bar reasoning also combines seven minus two y-bars.

items.prompt: Find the missing coefficient: 3k + ___k = 11k.
steps: Eleven equal k-bars must be made from three known bars and the missing bars.
11 − 3 = 8, so the missing term is 8k.

items.prompt: Do 2s + 6 + 3s and 5s + 6 always have equal values? Give a structural reason.
steps: The first expression has two s-bars plus three s-bars, which is five s-bars.
Both then add the same six units; the reasoning does not depend on a chosen s.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Combine like quantities
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A box has 3x red tokens and 2x blue tokens. Four tokens are removed. Express the remaining total.
steps: The colours together give 3x + 2x = 5x tokens.
Subtract the four removed tokens from that total.

items.prompt: A rope has segments of lengths 2a cm, 5a cm and 6 cm. Write its total length in simplest form.
steps: The first two segments combine to seven a-sized lengths.
The six-centimetre segment contributes a fixed 6 cm.

items.prompt: A learner says 5n − n = 5 because the letters cancel. Correct it.
steps: Subtract one n-bar from five, leaving four n-bars.
For n = 3, the original equals 15 − 3 = 12, consistent with 4n and not with 5.

items.prompt: Simplify 8c + 10 − 3c − 7, then check at c = 2.
steps: The c-terms give 5c and the numbers give 3.
At c = 2, both 16 + 10 − 6 − 7 and 10 + 3 equal 13.

items.prompt: Create two different expressions that simplify to 6z + 4.
steps: Both must have z-coefficients whose combined value is six.
Their fixed number terms must combine to four; other correct decompositions are valid.

items.prompt: A table has two rows: 2x + 7 and 3x + 5. Write their combined total and explain each term.
steps: The x-bars from both rows combine: 2x + 3x = 5x.
The fixed units combine: 7 + 5 = 12.

weeks.title: Substitute and evaluate
weeks.objective: Replace a letter by its stated value and follow the order of operations.

connection.before: Simplify simple linear expressions by collecting matching letter terms and numbers.
connection.after: S1 introduces signed coefficients, brackets, formulas and linear graphs.

days: Build or sketch a model for substitute and evaluate; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: An expression is a rule until the letter receives a value. If x = 4, the expression 3x + 2 means three groups of four plus two, so it gives 14. It does not mean the two-digit number 34 plus two; adjacent coefficient and letter indicate multiplication.

Complete multiplication or division before addition or subtraction. For 20 − 2x with x = 6, first calculate 2 × 6 = 12 and then subtract from 20. A bar picture shows the removed section as two x-sized groups, not as a sequence that subtracts 2 and then multiplies.

Keep the letter meaning and units attached to the situation. If x counts packets and 4x + 3 counts pens, its result is a pen count. Allowed values must fit the story: the expression 30 − 5x for money left after purchases requires 5x not to exceed 30.

examples.prompt: Evaluate 5x + 7 when x = 3.
steps: The expression contains five equal x-bars and seven separate units. The given x = 3 specifies the size of each bar, not the number of bars.
Replace each x by 3; 5x means 5 × 3 = 15.
Add 7 to get 22; multiply before adding or subtracting.

examples.prompt: Evaluate 8x − 9 when x = 4.
steps: The expression starts with eight equal x-bars, then removes nine fixed units. The given x = 4 labels each individual bar.
Replace each x by 4; 8x means 8 × 4 = 32.
Subtract 9 to get 23; multiply before adding or subtracting.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Substitute and evaluate
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Find 3x + 4 for x = 6.
steps: Replace each x by 6; 3x means 3 × 6 = 18.
Add 4 to get 22; multiply before adding or subtracting.

items.prompt: Evaluate 7x − 5 at x = 2.
steps: Replace each x by 2; 7x means 7 × 2 = 14.
Subtract 5 to get 9; multiply before adding or subtracting.

items.prompt: If x = 8, find 2x + 11.
steps: Replace each x by 8; 2x means 2 × 8 = 16.
Add 11 to get 27; multiply before adding or subtracting.

items.prompt: Find 24 − 3n when n = 5.
steps: The removed part is 3 × 5 = 15.
Subtract from 24: 24 − 15 = 9.

items.prompt: Evaluate p/4 + 3 for p = 20.
steps: Divide first: 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
Then add 3 to obtain 8.

items.prompt: A learner reads 6a as 64 when a = 4. Correct the evaluation.
steps: 6a means six groups of a, not digit joining.
Six groups of four give 6 × 4 = 24.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Substitute and evaluate
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A cost in dollars is 4x + 6. Find the cost for x = 7 tickets.
steps: Replace each x by 7; 4x means 4 × 7 = 28.
Add 6 to get 34; multiply before adding or subtracting.

items.prompt: A pattern has 5x − 2 tiles. Find its tile count when x = 9.
steps: Replace each x by 9; 5x means 5 × 9 = 45.
Subtract 2 to get 43; multiply before adding or subtracting.

items.prompt: For y = 3, evaluate 9y + 2y + 5 by simplifying first.
steps: Collect like terms: 9y + 2y + 5 = 11y + 5.
Substitute 3: 33 + 5 = 38.

items.prompt: Evaluate 40 − 6t for t = 4. Explain why subtracting 6 first is wrong.
steps: 6t is one product, so it is 6 × 4 = 24.
40 − 24 = 16; the expression does not instruct multiplying the entire difference by 4.

items.prompt: Find the values of 2n + 1 for n = 1, 2, 3. What changes each time?
steps: Substitute each n and double it before adding one.
Increasing n by one adds one extra pair, so the outputs grow by two.

items.prompt: Does x = 5 make 3x + 4 equal 19? Show the substitution.
steps: Replace x with 5 to obtain 3 × 5 + 4.
15 + 4 = 19, matching the required value.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Substitute and evaluate
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A pupil has $50 and spends $7 per notebook. The remaining money is 50 − 7n. Find it for n = 6.
steps: Six notebooks cost 7 × 6 = $42.
Subtract $42 from $50 to obtain $8.

items.prompt: A hall has 8x + 12 chairs. Find the total when x = 5 and explain what the 12 may represent.
items.answer: 52 chairs; for example 12 extra chairs outside the equal rows
steps: Five groups of eight contribute 40 chairs.
Add the fixed 12 chairs; any interpretation keeping the 12 fixed is valid.

items.prompt: A rectangle is 10 cm long and b cm wide. Its perimeter is 20 + 2b. Evaluate for b = 6.
steps: The two widths together contribute 2 × 6 = 12 cm.
Add the fixed 20 cm from the two lengths.

items.prompt: For c = 4, compare 5c + 3 and 3c + 9.
steps: The first gives 20 + 3 = 23.
The second gives 12 + 9 = 21, so the first exceeds the second by 2.

items.prompt: The number of full boxes is n and 24 − 4n counts unused bottles. Which values n = 4, 6, 7 are possible?
steps: The corresponding remainders are 8, 0 and −4.
A count cannot be negative, so seven full four-bottle boxes cannot be filled from 24 bottles.

items.prompt: Make an expression using 3x and a positive whole number that equals 20 when x = 4.
steps: At x = 4, the term 3x equals 12.
Eight more is needed to reach 20; substitute to check 12 + 8 = 20.

weeks.title: Simple equations from bars
weeks.objective: Solve a simple whole-number linear equation and check it in the original relationship.

connection.before: Replace a letter by its stated value and follow the order of operations.
connection.after: S1 introduces signed coefficients, brackets, formulas and linear graphs.

days: Build or sketch a model for simple equations from bars; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: An equation sets the value of an expression. In 4x + 3 = 31, draw four equal x-bars and a separate block of 3, together equal to 31. Remove the known block from the total: the four bars contain 28, so each bar is 7.

Undo operations in reverse order. If 5x − 6 = 29, add back the removed six to get 5x = 35, then divide by five. These steps preserve equality because they apply matching operations to both sides. Keep whole-number coefficients and simple equations within this Primary 6 work.

Always substitute into the original equation, including any added or removed amount. Finding x = 7 is not enough if the question asks for three boxes or the full perimeter. Interpret what x labels, then calculate the requested quantity and check the context.

examples.prompt: Solve 3x + 8 = 35.
steps: Draw three equal x-bars plus an eight-unit block, all bracketed as 35. The fixed block is outside the repeated unknown bars.
Undo the addition of 8: 3x = 27.
Divide by 3 to get x = 9; substitution gives 3 × 9 + 8 = 35.

examples.prompt: Solve 6x − 5 = 43.
steps: Six equal x-bars would form the complete amount before five were removed; adding those five back rebuilds the six-bar total.
Undo the subtraction of 5: 6x = 48.
Divide by 6 to get x = 8; substitution gives 6 × 8 − 5 = 43.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Simple equations from bars
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Solve 4x + 7 = 31.
steps: Undo the addition of 7: 4x = 24.
Divide by 4 to get x = 6; substitution gives 4 × 6 + 7 = 31.

items.prompt: Find x if 5x = 45.
steps: Undo the addition of 0: 5x = 45.
Divide by 5 to get x = 9; substitution gives 5 × 9 + 0 = 45.

items.prompt: Solve 2x − 9 = 17.
steps: Undo the subtraction of 9: 2x = 26.
Divide by 2 to get x = 13; substitution gives 2 × 13 − 9 = 17.

items.prompt: Solve x + 12 = 38.
steps: Remove the known twelve from both sides.
38 − 12 = 26; 26 + 12 = 38 checks the equation.

items.prompt: Solve x/3 = 7.
steps: One third of the x-bar is 7.
Three such parts total 3 × 7 = 21; 21 ÷ 3 = 7.

items.prompt: A learner solves 4x + 6 = 30 as x = 9 by adding 6 first. Correct the work.
steps: The added six must be removed: 4x = 30 − 6 = 24.
Divide by four; 4 × 6 + 6 = 30, while x = 9 gives 42.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Simple equations from bars
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Find the unknown in 7x + 2 = 58.
steps: Undo the addition of 2: 7x = 56.
Divide by 7 to get x = 8; substitution gives 7 × 8 + 2 = 58.

items.prompt: Solve 9x − 8 = 46.
steps: Undo the subtraction of 8: 9x = 54.
Divide by 9 to get x = 6; substitution gives 9 × 6 − 8 = 46.

items.prompt: Three equal packets and 4 loose cards total 40 cards. Find cards per packet.
steps: Let x be cards per packet: 3x + 4 = 40.
Remove four, then divide by three: x = 36 ÷ 3 = 12.

items.prompt: A cord is cut into 5 equal pieces after 7 cm is removed. Each piece is 9 cm. Find the original length.
steps: The five equal pieces total 5 × 9 = 45 cm.
Add back the removed 7 cm: original length = 52 cm.

items.prompt: Does x = 4 solve 8x + 3 = 36? Explain.
steps: Substitute: 8 × 4 + 3 = 35.
The left side is one below 36, so equality does not hold.

items.prompt: Two identical boxes and 11 loose pencils hold 37 pencils. Write and solve the equation.
steps: The two box-bars total 37 − 11 = 26 pencils.
Split 26 equally between two boxes; 2 × 13 + 11 = 37.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Simple equations from bars
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A notebook costs $x. Four notebooks and a $5 pen cost $33. Find the cost of six notebooks.
steps: Six notebooks cost 6 × $7 = $42; the pen is not part of the requested purchase.

items.prompt: A rectangle has width x cm and length 12 cm. Its perimeter is 40 cm. Find x.
steps: The two lengths use 24 cm, leaving 16 cm for the two widths.

items.prompt: A team buys 7 equal-price balls for $63 and pays a separate $8 delivery fee. Find the price per ball and the total bill.
steps: The $63 labels only the seven ball prices, so each costs 63 ÷ 7 = $9.
Add the separate delivery fee to $63 to get $71.

items.prompt: A learner finds x = 5 for 3x − 4 = 11. Explain a bar check.
items.answer: Three five-unit bars total 15; removing 4 leaves 11.
steps: Rebuild the full 3x amount as 3 × 5 = 15.
Subtract the four-unit section to recover the stated 11.

items.prompt: Write a simple equation with solution x = 6 using coefficient 5 and an added positive whole number.
steps: At x = 6, five equal x-bars total 30.
Choose an added number such as 2 and make the right side 32; other matching choices work.

items.prompt: The equation 4x + 9 = 41 models four bags and nine loose marbles. Explain what x is and find the marbles in two bags.
items.answer: x is marbles per bag; two bags hold 16 marbles.
steps: Remove nine from 41 and divide by four to get x = 8.
The requested two bags hold 2 × 8 = 16; all four bags plus nine give 41.

weeks.title: Radius, diameter and circumference
weeks.objective: Distinguish circle measurements and calculate circumference from a radius or diameter.

connection.before: Solve a simple whole-number linear equation and check it in the original relationship.
connection.after: S1 extends composite measures and later secondary work generalises circular sectors.

days: Build or sketch a model for radius, diameter and circumference; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: A radius joins the centre of a circle to any point on its boundary. A diameter passes through the centre and joins two boundary points, so it contains two radii. A string laid once around a circular lid measures its circumference, which is a length, not an area.

The ratio of circumference to diameter is π. Thus C = πd and, because d = 2r, C = 2πr. Use the stated approximation of π consistently. With π = 22/7 and diameter 14 cm, circumference is 44 cm; the actual circle measurement is approximated by the chosen value of π.

Do not double a supplied diameter a second time. Draw a centre mark and label whether the given segment reaches one side or both sides. A reasonable circumference is a little more than three diameters. For a path repeated several times, find one complete circumference before multiplying by the number of laps.

examples.prompt: A circle has radius 7 cm. Find its circumference. Use π = 22/7.
steps: The given 7 cm goes from the centre to the circle edge, so the full diameter is 14 cm.
The radius is 7 cm, so the full-circle circumference is 2 × (22/7) × 7 = 44 cm.
Check the scale: diameter 14 cm times 3 is 42 cm, so 44 cm is a little more than three diameters, as circumference should be.

examples.prompt: A circular lid has diameter 21 cm. Find its circumference. Use π = 22/7.
steps: The given 21 cm crosses the circle through its centre. It is already a diameter, so use πd without doubling it.
The radius is 10.5 cm, so the full-circle circumference is 2 × (22/7) × 10.5 = 66 cm.
Check the scale: three diameters total 63 cm, so the 66 cm circumference is slightly larger and has length units.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Radius, diameter and circumference
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Find the circumference of a circle with diameter 28 cm. Use π = 22/7.
steps: The radius is 14 cm, so the full-circle circumference is 2 × (22/7) × 14 = 88 cm.
Take the whole of that measure: 88 cm.

items.prompt: A wheel has radius 3.5 cm. Find the distance around it. Use π = 22/7.
steps: The radius is 3.5 cm, so the full-circle circumference is 2 × (22/7) × 3.5 = 22 cm.
Take the whole of that measure: 22 cm.

items.prompt: A circle has radius 9 cm. Find its diameter.
steps: A diameter contains two equal radii.

items.prompt: A circular sign has diameter 32 cm. Find the centre-to-edge distance.
steps: The centre-to-edge distance is a radius.
Halve the diameter: 32 ÷ 2 = 16 cm.

items.prompt: Name the circle measure found by wrapping a string once around a lid.
steps: The string follows the curved boundary.
It measures a length around the circle, not the distance through its centre or the covered area.

items.prompt: A learner uses 2π × 20 for a diameter of 20 cm. Correct the formula.
steps: The formula 2πr requires a radius, which would be 10 cm.
For the given diameter, use πd directly; doubling 20 counts twice the circumference.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Radius, diameter and circumference
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Find the circumference when the radius is 21 cm. Use π = 22/7.
steps: The radius is 21 cm, so the full-circle circumference is 2 × (22/7) × 21 = 132 cm.
Take the whole of that measure: 132 cm.

items.prompt: A disc has diameter 35 cm. Find its circumference. Use π = 22/7.
steps: The radius is 17.5 cm, so the full-circle circumference is 2 × (22/7) × 17.5 = 110 cm.
Take the whole of that measure: 110 cm.

items.prompt: Using π = 22/7, a circle has circumference 88 cm. Find its diameter.
steps: The circumference equals (22/7) times the diameter.

items.prompt: A circle circumference is 66 cm using π = 22/7. Find its radius.
steps: First find diameter: 66 × 7/22 = 21 cm.
The radius is half of 21 cm, or 10.5 cm.

items.prompt: Two circles have diameters 7 cm and 14 cm. How do their circumferences compare?
items.answer: The second circumference is twice the first.
steps: Both circumferences are π times the diameter.
Doubling the diameter doubles that product: 22 cm becomes 44 cm using π = 22/7.

items.prompt: Would 20 cm be a reasonable circumference for a diameter of 10 cm? Explain without exact calculation.
steps: The circumference should be a little more than three diameters.
Three diameters already total 30 cm, so 20 cm is too small.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Radius, diameter and circumference
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A circular wire loop has diameter 42 cm. Using π = 22/7, find the length of wire for 3 such loops without overlaps.
steps: One loop needs (22/7) × 42 = 132 cm.
Three separate loops need 3 × 132 = 396 cm.

explanation: Cutting a circle into many thin wedges and alternating their directions suggests a rectangle-like shape. Its height is the radius and its long side approaches half the circumference. This connects area to πr × r, giving A = πr². The formula measures the surface covered, in square units.

If a diameter is given, halve it before calculating the area. For diameter 14 cm, radius is 7 cm, so using π = 22/7 gives area 22/7 × 7 × 7 = 154 cm². Multiplying π by the diameter squared would make the area four times too large.

Doubling radius doubles both dimensions of the covering, so area is multiplied by four. Circumference only doubles. Check area against a square that contains the circle: a circle of diameter d fits inside a d-by-d square, so its area must be below d².
