explanation: A diameter cuts a circle into two equal semicircular regions. Each region covers half the full-circle area, and its curved edge is half the full circumference. This gives semicircle area = πr²/2 and arc length = πr.

The perimeter of the region also includes its straight diameter. Trace the whole boundary with a finger: travel around the curved arc, then along the diameter back to the start. Thus semicircle perimeter = πr + 2r. The straight edge contributes length but no additional area.

When a semicircle is attached along its diameter to another shape, that shared edge may become internal and no longer belong to the outside perimeter. Mark exposed edges before adding lengths. Use the given diameter to find the radius and keep area and boundary calculations separate.

steps: A diameter divides the radius-7 cm circle into two equal regions; the required area is one of those halves.

Take half of that measure: 77 cm².

examples.prompt: A semicircular region has diameter 28 cm. Find its full perimeter, including the straight edge. Use π = 22/7.

Take half of that measure and add 28 cm of straight boundary: 72 cm.

explanation: Plan an area calculation by splitting a figure into non-overlapping familiar pieces, or by subtracting holes from a containing region. connection.before: Decompose a fully described figure and count only exposed boundary edges.
connection.after: S1 extends root reasoning and volume to prisms and cylinders.

days: Build or sketch a model for recover base area and height; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: Build a cuboid from 1 cm cubes. If the base contains 24 cubes and there are 5 layers, the volume is 24 × 5 = 120 cm³. The base area tells how many square-centimetre positions are in each layer; the height tells how many centimetre-thick layers there are.

The relationship is volume = base area × perpendicular height. To recover height, divide volume by base area. To recover base area, divide volume by height. Units explain the difference: cm³ ÷ cm² gives cm, while cm³ ÷ cm gives cm².

Do not divide by a side length when the problem asks for height unless the other base dimension has also been included. Check an inverse calculation by rebuilding the original volume. A tank problem uses internal dimensions unless stated otherwise; outside measurements alone do not determine its capacity.

examples.prompt: A cuboid volume is 360 cm³ and its height is 9 cm. Find its base area.
steps: Think of the solid as nine one-centimetre layers of identical base area. Together those layers contain 360 cubic centimetres.
Share 360 cm³ among the nine equal one-centimetre layers: 360 ÷ 9 = 40 cm³ per layer, corresponding to base area 40 cm².
Rebuild the volume: 40 cm² × 9 cm = 360 cm³. The recovered quantity is an area, so use cm².

examples.prompt: A tank has base area 48 cm² and volume 336 cm³. Find its height.
steps: A one-centimetre layer over the 48 cm² base holds 48 cm³; the unknown height counts how many such layers make 336 cm³.
Divide the total volume by one layer volume: 336 ÷ 48 = 7, so seven one-centimetre layers fit.
The height is 7 cm; check that 48 cm² × 7 cm = 336 cm³ restores the stated volume.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Recover base area and height
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Find the base area of a cuboid with volume 240 cm³ and height 6 cm.
steps: Every 1 cm layer has the same base area; 6 layers make the given volume.
Base area = 240 ÷ 6 = 40 cm²; multiplying by height restores 240 cm³.

items.prompt: A solid has volume 525 cm³ and uniform height 7 cm over a rectangular base. Find the base area.
steps: Every 1 cm layer has the same base area; 7 layers make the given volume.
Base area = 525 ÷ 7 = 75 cm²; multiplying by height restores 525 cm³.

items.prompt: A cuboid has base area 30 cm² and volume 270 cm³. Find its height.
steps: Use volume = base area × height.
270 ÷ 30 = 9 cm; nine layers of 30 cm³ make the total.

items.prompt: A stack has 12 layers, each covering 15 cm² and 1 cm high. Find its volume.
steps: Each layer occupies 15 cm³.
Twelve identical layers occupy 12 × 15 = 180 cm³.

items.prompt: Which unit belongs to 480 cm³ ÷ 12 cm: cm or cm²? Explain.
steps: The division removes one length dimension from a volume.
It recovers the area of the equal layers, here 40 cm².

items.prompt: A learner divides volume 200 cm³ by height 5 cm and labels the answer 40 cm. Correct the unit.
steps: Volume divided by height gives base area.
The numerical value 200 ÷ 5 = 40 is correct, but the area requires square centimetres.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Recover base area and height
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A tank volume is 864 cm³ and its internal height is 12 cm. Find the base area.
steps: Every 1 cm layer has the same base area; 12 layers make the given volume.
Base area = 864 ÷ 12 = 72 cm²; multiplying by height restores 864 cm³.

items.prompt: A rectangular tank has base area 84 cm². Water volume is 504 cm³. Find water depth.
steps: The depth is the number of 1 cm layers above the base.
504 ÷ 84 = 6 cm; use water volume, not total tank capacity.

items.prompt: Two cuboids have equal volume 600 cm³. Their base areas are 60 cm² and 100 cm². Find their heights.
steps: For the first, 600 ÷ 60 = 10 cm.
For the second, 600 ÷ 100 = 6 cm; a larger base needs fewer layers for the same volume.

items.prompt: A cuboid has base area 45 cm² and height 8 cm. A learner claims its volume is 360 cm³. Check by division.
steps: Divide the claimed volume by its height: 360 ÷ 8 = 45 cm².
This matches the stated base area; equivalently 45 × 8 = 360.

items.prompt: A volume of 420 cm³ is arranged in layers over a 70 cm² base. How much volume does one extra 1 cm layer add?
steps: Each 1 cm layer has volume base area × 1 cm.
Thus every added layer contributes 70 cm³, regardless of the existing six layers.

items.prompt: A cuboid volume is 288 cm³ and its height doubles while the base stays fixed. Find the new volume.
steps: Twice as many identical layers are stacked.
The volume doubles: 288 × 2 = 576 cm³.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Recover base area and height
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A tank has 100 cm² base area and water depth 7 cm. It receives 300 cm³ more water without overflowing. Find the new depth.
steps: The added water raises the depth by 300 ÷ 100 = 3 cm.
Add this to the original depth: 7 + 3 = 10 cm.

items.prompt: A cuboid has volume 720 cm³. If its height is reduced from 12 cm to 9 cm with the same base, find the new volume.
steps: The base area is 720 ÷ 12 = 60 cm².
Nine layers give 60 × 9 = 540 cm³.

items.prompt: A tank has internal height 20 cm and capacity 2400 cm³. It is filled to half its height. Find base area and water volume.
steps: Base area = 2400 ÷ 20 = 120 cm².
Half height is 10 cm, so volume = 120 × 10 = 1200 cm³.

items.prompt: Give two different base-area and height pairs that make volume 180 cm³.
items.answer: For example, 30 cm² with 6 cm and 45 cm² with 4 cm
steps: Each pair must multiply to 180 cm³.
30 × 6 = 180 and 45 × 4 = 180; other positive pairs are valid.

items.prompt: A cuboid has base area 32 cm² and volume 256 cm³. A lid is 2 cm above the top of the solid. Find the lid height above the base.
steps: The solid height is 256 ÷ 32 = 8 cm.
The lid is 2 cm higher, so its height above the base is 10 cm.

items.prompt: A cuboid volume is 600 cm³ and its base area is unknown. Is its height determined? Explain with two examples.
steps: A 60 cm² base gives height 10 cm.
A 100 cm² base gives height 6 cm; both have the stated volume.

weeks.title: Find a missing cuboid dimension
weeks.objective: Recover an unknown side length from volume and the other two dimensions.

connection.before: Use volume as equal layers to find a missing base area or height.
connection.after: S1 extends root reasoning and volume to prisms and cylinders.

days: Build or sketch a model for find a missing cuboid dimension; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: Choose the face whose two dimensions are known. For volume 480 cm³ with length 10 cm and width 6 cm, the base contains 60 square centimetres. Each centimetre of height adds 60 cm³, so the missing height is 480 ÷ 60 = 8 cm.

The same method works when width or length is missing. Reorder the three factors to group the two known lengths, then divide volume by their product. A labelled box sketch helps prevent using one dimension twice or mistaking a face area for a side length.

For a fixed volume, many different triples of dimensions are possible. If one dimension doubles while another remains fixed, the third must halve. Check all three factors and the length units, and use internal measurements when determining how much a container holds.

examples.prompt: A cuboid has volume 840 cm³, length 14 cm and width 10 cm. Find its height.
steps: Use the known 14 cm by 10 cm face as the base; the missing height counts equal layers above it.
The known face area is 14 × 10 = 140 cm².
Divide volume by this area: 840 ÷ 140 = 6 cm; rebuilding the product gives 840 cm³.

examples.prompt: A box has volume 540 cm³, height 9 cm and width 5 cm. Find its length.
steps: The known 9 cm height and 5 cm width form a rectangular end face. The missing length counts how many centimetre-thick slabs extend from that face.
The known face area is 9 × 5 = 45 cm².
Divide volume by this area: 540 ÷ 45 = 12 cm; rebuilding the product gives 540 cm³.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Find a missing cuboid dimension
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Find the missing height of a 12 cm by 5 cm cuboid with volume 420 cm³.
steps: The known face area is 12 × 5 = 60 cm².
Divide volume by this area: 420 ÷ 60 = 7 cm; rebuilding the product gives 420 cm³.

items.prompt: A cuboid volume is 384 cm³. Its length is 8 cm and height is 6 cm. Find width.
steps: The known face area is 8 × 6 = 48 cm².
Divide volume by this area: 384 ÷ 48 = 8 cm; rebuilding the product gives 384 cm³.

items.prompt: A tank has internal base dimensions 20 cm by 15 cm and capacity 3600 cm³. Find internal height.
steps: The known face area is 20 × 15 = 300 cm².
Divide volume by this area: 3600 ÷ 300 = 12 cm; rebuilding the product gives 3600 cm³.

items.prompt: A box has volume 360 cm³ and dimensions 10 cm, 6 cm and x cm. Write the equation for x.
steps: The known face area is 10 × 6 = 60 cm².
Volume is 60 times the missing length, so divide 360 by 60.

items.prompt: A learner uses 600 ÷ 10 = 60 cm as a missing height when volume is 600 cm³ and base is 10 cm by 5 cm. Correct it.
steps: The base area is 10 × 5 = 50 cm², not just 10 cm.

items.prompt: A cuboid has volume 144 cm³ and two sides of 6 cm each. Find the third side.
steps: The known face covers 6 × 6 = 36 cm².

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Find a missing cuboid dimension
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A cuboid volume is 990 cm³. Its width is 9 cm and height is 10 cm. Find length.
steps: The known face area is 9 × 10 = 90 cm².
Divide volume by this area: 990 ÷ 90 = 11 cm; rebuilding the product gives 990 cm³.

items.prompt: A box with volume 315 cm³ has a 7 cm by 6 cm base. Find height.
steps: The known face area is 7 × 6 = 42 cm².
Divide volume by this area: 315 ÷ 42 = 7.5 cm; rebuilding the product gives 315 cm³.

items.prompt: A 10 cm by 8 cm by 6 cm cuboid is reshaped into another cuboid with base 12 cm by 10 cm, with volume unchanged. Find its height.
steps: The original volume is 10 × 8 × 6 = 480 cm³.
The new base area is 120 cm²; 480 ÷ 120 = 4 cm.

items.prompt: A cuboid has volume 720 cm³, width 8 cm and height 9 cm. Is a proposed length of 12 cm correct?
steps: The proposed dimensions give 12 × 8 × 9 = 864 cm³.
To match 720 cm³, divide 720 by 8 × 9 = 72 to get 10 cm.

items.prompt: A box has length 16 cm, width 5 cm and height 6 cm. Keeping volume and width fixed, its length becomes 8 cm. Find the new height.
steps: Halving the length halves each layer area.
The height must double from 6 to 12 cm to preserve volume; 8 × 5 × 12 = 480 cm³.

items.prompt: A cuboid volume is 180 cm³ and length is 9 cm. Find the area of the face perpendicular to the length.
steps: That face area multiplied by the length gives the volume.
180 ÷ 9 = 20 cm²; its two individual dimensions are not determined.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Find a missing cuboid dimension
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A rectangular tank has base 25 cm by 12 cm and contains 4500 cm³ of water. Find the water depth.
steps: The base area is 25 × 12 = 300 cm².
Water depth = 4500 ÷ 300 = 15 cm.

items.prompt: A box has width 4 cm and height 6 cm. Its volume increases from 192 to 288 cm³ by changing only its length. How much longer is it?
steps: The fixed face area is 24 cm²; lengths are 192 ÷ 24 = 8 and 288 ÷ 24 = 12 cm.
Subtract the old length from the new: 12 − 8 = 4 cm.

items.prompt: A solid cuboid has volume 252 cm³, length 9 cm and width 7 cm. It is stacked on a 3 cm high stand. Find total height.
steps: The cuboid height is 252 ÷ 63 = 4 cm.
Add the stand height: 4 + 3 = 7 cm.

items.prompt: Find two different whole-number widths and heights for a cuboid of volume 240 cm³ and length 10 cm.
items.answer: For example, 3 cm by 8 cm and 4 cm by 6 cm
steps: The width-height product must be 240 ÷ 10 = 24 cm².
Both 3 × 8 and 4 × 6 equal 24; other positive factor pairs are valid.

items.prompt: A cuboid of volume 800 cm³ must have height 10 cm and width 8 cm. Can its length be below 9 cm?
steps: The known face area is 10 × 8 = 80 cm².
800 ÷ 80 = 10 cm is the unique length meeting all three conditions.

items.prompt: A container outer dimensions are 12 cm by 10 cm by 8 cm. Can its exact liquid capacity be found if wall thickness is unknown?
steps: The product 960 cm³ measures the entire outer box.
The interior is smaller by an unknown amount; internal dimensions or wall thickness are needed.

weeks.title: Cube edges and roots
weeks.objective: Recover a cube edge from a perfect-cube volume and a square side from its area.

connection.before: Recover an unknown side length from volume and the other two dimensions.
connection.after: S1 extends root reasoning and volume to prisms and cylinders.

days: Build or sketch a model for cube edges and roots; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: A cube has the same length on all three edges meeting at a corner. If the edge is s cm, each layer has s² square-centimetre positions and there are s layers, so V = s³. To undo this, find the positive number whose cube equals the volume; this is the cube root, written ∛V.

For volume 125 cm³, try familiar whole-number edges: 4³ = 64 and 5³ = 125, so the edge is 5 cm. A square face with area 49 cm² instead needs the square root: √49 = 7 cm. Square roots undo two equal factors; cube roots undo three.

Dividing a cube volume by three does not find its edge. The three dimensions multiply; they do not add. Verify an edge by multiplying it three times and verify a face side by squaring it. This work uses perfect squares and cubes so the recovered lengths can be checked exactly.

examples.prompt: A cube has volume 216 cm³. Find its edge length.
steps: A cube uses the same unknown edge in its length, width and height, so its 216 cm³ volume has three equal length factors.
All three factors are the same edge s, so s × s × s = 216.

examples.prompt: A cube has one face of area 64 cm². Find its edge and volume.
steps: The 64 cm² face is a square, so first recover its equal side lengths; that same side is also the height of the cube.
The square face gives edge √64 = 8 cm.
The cube volume is 8 × 8 × 8 = 512 cm³.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Cube edges and roots
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Find the edge of a cube with volume 27 cm³.
steps: A cube has three equal edge factors.
3 × 3 × 3 = 27, so the positive cube root is 3.

items.prompt: A cube volume is 343 cm³. Find the edge.
steps: The edge is the positive number whose cube is 343.
7 × 7 × 7 = 343 confirms 7 cm.

items.prompt: Find the side of a square base of area 81 cm².
steps: Equal side lengths multiply to make the square area.

items.prompt: Evaluate ∛1000 and explain what it means for a cube measured in centimetres.
items.answer: 10; a 1000 cm³ cube has 10 cm edges
steps: The cube root recovers one of the three equal length factors.

items.prompt: A learner finds the edge of a 64 cm³ cube by calculating 64 ÷ 3. Correct the method.
steps: Volume is a product of three equal lengths, not their sum.
4 × 4 × 4 = 64; dividing by three cannot undo cubing.

items.prompt: A cube has edge 9 cm. Find its volume to check a claim of 729 cm³.
steps: One layer has 9 × 9 = 81 square-centimetre positions.
Nine layers give 81 × 9 = 729 cm³.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Cube edges and roots
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Find the edge of a cube with volume 1728 cm³.
steps: The edge must cube to 1728.

items.prompt: A cube has face area 25 cm². Find its volume.
steps: The edge is √25 = 5 cm.
The volume is 5³ = 125 cm³.

items.prompt: A cuboid is 12 cm by 6 cm by 3 cm. A cube has the same volume. Find the cube edge.
steps: The cuboid volume is 12 × 6 × 3 = 216 cm³.
The positive cube root of 216 is 6 cm.

items.prompt: A cube has volume 512 cm³. Find the area of one face.
steps: Its edge is 8 cm because 8³ = 512.
One square face has area 8 × 8 = 64 cm².

items.prompt: A cube edge doubles from 3 cm to 6 cm. By what factor does volume grow?
steps: The three edge factors each double.
The volume factor is 2 × 2 × 2 = 8; 27 cm³ becomes 216 cm³.

items.prompt: Which is appropriate for a cube of volume 125 cm³: √125 or ∛125? Explain.
steps: A cube volume multiplies three equal edges.
The cube root reverses that operation and gives edge 5 cm; a square root reverses two factors.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Cube edges and roots
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Eight identical cubes of volume 27 cm³ are arranged as a 2-by-2-by-2 larger cube with no gaps. Find the large cube edge.
steps: Each small cube edge is 3 cm.
Two small edges span each large edge, so it is 2 × 3 = 6 cm.

items.prompt: A cube of edge 10 cm is melted and recast into cubes of edge 5 cm without loss. How many small cubes form?
steps: The starting volume is 1000 cm³ and each new cube is 125 cm³.
1000 ÷ 125 = 8; all material is accounted for.

items.prompt: A cube has volume 729 cm³. It is placed on a 4 cm tall stand. Find the total height.
steps: The cube edge is ∛729 = 9 cm.
Add the stand: 9 + 4 = 13 cm.

items.prompt: A square-based cuboid has base area 49 cm² and volume 392 cm³. Is it a cube?
items.answer: No; its dimensions are 7 cm, 7 cm, 8 cm.
steps: The square base side is √49 = 7 cm.
The height is 392 ÷ 49 = 8 cm, which differs from the base side.

items.prompt: A cube edge is a whole number and its volume is between 100 and 200 cm³. Find the edge.
steps: 4³ = 64 is too small and 6³ = 216 is too large.
5³ = 125 lies between the limits, so edge 5 cm is the only whole-number choice.

items.prompt: Compare a cube of volume 64 cm³ with a cuboid of length 8 cm, width 4 cm and height 2 cm. Are both their volumes and heights necessarily the same?
items.answer: Volumes are equal; with the stated 2 cm cuboid height, heights differ.
steps: The cube edge is 4 cm and both volumes are 64 cm³.
A volume alone does not determine shape or height; the cuboid height here is 2 cm.

weeks.title: Water depths and transferred volume
weeks.objective: Convert liquid units and use conservation of volume to recover water depths.

connection.before: Recover a cube edge from a perfect-cube volume and a square side from its area.
connection.after: S1 extends root reasoning and volume to prisms and cylinders.

days: Build or sketch a model for water depths and transferred volume; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: Liquid volume can be counted in cubic centimetres: 1 mL = 1 cm³ and 1 L = 1000 cm³. A rectangular tank with base 20 cm by 10 cm holds 200 cm³ in each 1 cm layer. Converting a 3 L supply to 3000 cm³ lets us find depth as 3000 ÷ 200 = 15 cm.

When water is transferred without spilling, the volume leaving one container equals the volume entering the other. Depth usually changes because the base areas differ. Find the transferred volume from one tank, then divide it by the receiving tank base area; check that the receiving tank is tall enough.

A rise or fall in level depends on the change in volume, not automatically on the total capacity. Treat each stated condition separately: current depth, added volume, maximum height and any remainder. Measurements here are internal and tanks have vertical rectangular walls.

examples.prompt: A tank has internal base 20 cm by 15 cm and contains 4.5 L. Find water depth.
steps: Represent the water as equal 1 cm layers over the 20 cm by 15 cm internal base. Convert the liquid amount to cubic centimetres to count these layers.
Convert 4.5 L to 4500 cm³; the base area is 300 cm².

examples.prompt: Water 8 cm deep in a tank with base 15 cm by 10 cm is poured into an empty tank with base 20 cm by 12 cm, tall enough to hold it. Find the new depth.
steps: The first tank gives a known rectangular water block. Pouring without loss preserves that block volume even though the receiving base has a different area.
The conserved water volume is 15 × 10 × 8 = 1200 cm³.
The receiving base area is 240 cm², so depth is 1200 ÷ 240 = 5 cm.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Water depths and transferred volume
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Convert 2.8 L to cm³.
steps: Each litre contains 1000 mL.
Each millilitre equals 1 cm³, so multiply 2.8 by 1000.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

items.prompt: A tank base area is 80 cm² and water volume is 640 mL. Find depth.
steps: 640 mL equals 640 cm³.
Divide by the base area: 640 ÷ 80 = 8 cm.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

items.prompt: A 25 cm by 8 cm tank base supports 6 cm of water. Find the water volume in litres.
steps: Volume is 25 × 8 × 6 = 1200 cm³.
Divide by 1000 to convert to litres.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

items.prompt: A tank base area is 150 cm². Add 300 mL with no overflow. How much does its water level rise?
steps: The added volume is 300 cm³.
Level rise = added volume ÷ base area = 300 ÷ 150 = 2 cm.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

items.prompt: A learner converts 1.5 L to 150 cm³. Correct it.
steps: One litre is 1000 cm³.
Multiply 1.5 by 1000, not by 100, to preserve the volume.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

items.prompt: Two empty tanks have base areas 100 cm² and 200 cm². Each receives 1 L. Compare water depths.
steps: 1 L is 1000 cm³, giving depths 1000/100 and 1000/200.
The tank with twice the base area has half the water depth.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Water depths and transferred volume
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A tank base is 30 cm by 20 cm and water is 12 cm deep. Remove 1.8 L. Find the new depth.
steps: The removed 1800 cm³ corresponds to 1800 ÷ 600 = 3 cm of depth.
Subtract the 3 cm fall from the initial 12 cm.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

items.prompt: A tank has base area 250 cm² and height 20 cm. It contains 3 L. How many litres more fill it?
steps: Full capacity is 250 × 20 = 5000 cm³ = 5 L.
Subtract the current 3 L from capacity to obtain 2 L.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

items.prompt: A cube-shaped tank has internal edge 10 cm. How many litres fill it?
steps: Capacity is 10³ = 1000 cm³.
1000 cm³ equals 1000 mL, or 1 L.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

items.prompt: A tank base is 18 cm by 10 cm. Removing water lowers its level by 5 cm. Find the amount removed in mL.
steps: The lost layer volume is 18 × 10 × 5 = 900 cm³.
Convert using 1 cm³ = 1 mL, giving 900 mL.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

items.prompt: A 2 L supply is poured into an empty tank with base 20 cm by 10 cm and height 8 cm. How much overflows?
steps: The tank capacity is 20 × 10 × 8 = 1600 cm³ = 1.6 L.
The excess is 2 − 1.6 = 0.4 L.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

items.prompt: A tank contains 1800 cm³ at depth 9 cm. Find its base area.
steps: Volume is base area times depth.
1800 ÷ 9 = 200 cm²; multiplying by 9 recovers the volume.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Water depths and transferred volume
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A tank with base 40 cm by 25 cm has water depth 6 cm. All water is moved to a tank with base 30 cm by 20 cm, height 15 cm. Find the new depth and check that it fits.
steps: Water volume is 40 × 25 × 6 = 6000 cm³.
New depth is 6000 ÷ 600 = 10 cm, below the 15 cm tank height.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

items.prompt: A tank base area is 120 cm². A tap adds 240 mL per minute for 3 minutes, with no overflow. Find the level rise.
steps: The added volume is 240 × 3 = 720 cm³.
Divide 720 by 120 to obtain a 6 cm rise.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

items.prompt: A tank has 2 L at depth 8 cm. Its width is 10 cm. Find its internal length.
steps: Convert to 2000 cm³; volume = length × 10 × 8.
Length = 2000 ÷ 80 = 25 cm.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

items.prompt: A 30 cm by 10 cm tank has depth 4 cm. Another tank pours in 900 mL. Find the final volume and depth, assuming sufficient height.
steps: The initial volume is 30 × 10 × 4 = 1200 mL; add 900 to get 2100 mL.
Divide 2100 cm³ by the 300 cm² base to obtain 7 cm.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

items.prompt: A tank contains 4 L. One quarter is removed and the rest fills a 15 cm by 20 cm tank. Find the new depth if none spills.
steps: Three quarters of 4 L is 3 L = 3000 cm³.
The receiving base is 300 cm², so depth is 3000 ÷ 300 = 10 cm.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

items.prompt: A pupil transfers water between tanks and says depth must stay unchanged because water volume is conserved. Give a numerical counterexample.
items.answer: For example, 1000 cm³ has depths 10 cm over 100 cm² and 5 cm over 200 cm².
steps: Both products, 100 × 10 and 200 × 5, equal 1000 cm³.
Conserved volume allows different depths when base areas differ.
items.skill: Liquid units and inverse tank volume

weeks.title: Link angle facts in a diagram
weeks.objective: Use straight-line, point, opposite-angle and triangle totals in a sequence of deductions.

connection.before: Convert liquid units and use conservation of volume to recover water depths.
connection.after: Secondary geometry formalises proof; statistics compares several measures of centre.

days: Build or sketch a model for link angle facts in a diagram; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: Angles sharing a straight line total 180°, and angles around one point total 360°. These are totals of turns, so the pieces must neither overlap nor leave gaps. When two straight lines cross, opposite angles are equal; adjacent angles on a straight line are supplementary.

The interior angles of a triangle total 180°. A composite diagram often needs one fact to supply a missing angle before another fact can be used. If a triangle angle is adjacent to an outside 120° angle on a straight line, its interior angle is 60°; combine that with the other triangle angles next.

Read every relationship from the labels and description rather than from the apparent shape. Name the reason for each deduction. All lines needed for these questions are already described; do not add a new line or assume two unmarked sides or angles are equal.

examples.prompt: A, B and D lie in that order on a straight line. Triangle ABC has angle A = 48° and exterior angle CBD = 126°. Find angle C.
steps: At B, rays BA and BD point in opposite directions. The outside 126° angle and the unknown interior angle therefore fill one straight angle.
At B, angle ABC = 180° − 126° = 54° because BA and BD are opposite rays.
In triangle ABC, C = 180° − 48° − 54° = 78°.

examples.prompt: Two lines AB and CD cross at O. Angle AOC = 68°. P lies on ray OB and Q lies on ray OD, forming triangle POQ with angle P = 47°. Find angle Q.
steps: The crossing lines make AOC and BOD vertically opposite. Rays OP and OQ follow OB and OD, so the triangle angle at O equals BOD.
Vertically opposite angles give BOD = AOC = 68°.
The triangle sum gives Q = 180° − 68° − 47° = 65°.

items.prompt: Triangle ABC has angles A = 57° and B = 64°. Find C.
steps: The three interior angles of a triangle total 180°.
Subtract the two known angles: 180° − 57° − 64° = 59°.

items.prompt: Three adjacent angles on a straight line are 35°, 82° and x. Find x.
steps: Their total is 180° because they exactly fill a straight angle.

items.prompt: Four angles around O are 90°, 115°, 85° and x, with no gaps or overlaps. Find x.
steps: A full turn around O is 360°.
Subtract the three known angles: 360 − 90 − 115 − 85 = 70°.

items.prompt: Two straight lines cross. One angle is 73°. Find its vertically opposite angle and either adjacent angle.
steps: Vertically opposite angles are equal.
An adjacent angle shares a straight line: 180° − 73° = 107°.

items.prompt: A right triangle has one other angle 38°. Find the remaining angle.
steps: The three interior angles of a triangle total 180°.
Subtract the two known angles: 180° − 90° − 38° = 52°.

items.prompt: A learner claims angles 70°, 65° and 55° form a triangle. Check.
steps: Their sum is 70 + 65 + 55 = 190°.
A triangle requires exactly 180°, so these three cannot be its interior angles.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Link angle facts in a diagram
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A, B, D are collinear with B between A and D. Triangle ABC has A = 35° and angle CBD = 110°. Find C.
steps: The interior angle at B is 180° − 110° = 70°.
The triangle sum gives C = 180° − 35° − 70° = 75°.

items.prompt: Triangle XYZ has X = 42° and Y = 68°. Side YZ is extended beyond Z to W. Find exterior angle XZW.
steps: The interior angle Z is 180° − 42° − 68° = 70°.
The exterior angle shares a straight line with Z, so it is 180° − 70° = 110°.

items.prompt: A triangle has two equal angles and its third angle is 44°. Find either equal angle.
steps: The two equal angles total 180° − 44° = 136°.
Share 136° equally: 136° ÷ 2 = 68°.

items.prompt: Two triangles ABC and CBD share BC and lie on opposite sides of it. In ABC, A = 50° and B = 60°. In CBD, C = 40° and D = 75°. Find angle ACD, made of ACB and BCD.
steps: At C the requested angle is 70° + 40° = 110°, since the triangles lie on opposite sides of BC.

items.prompt: Angle AOB is a right angle. Ray OC lies strictly inside it and angle AOC is 28°. Find COB.
steps: The two non-overlapping angles together fill 90°.

items.prompt: A learner assumes two triangle angles are equal because the sketch looks symmetric. No equal sides or angles are marked. Is the deduction justified?
steps: Visual appearance is not a stated geometric condition.
An equality needs a supplied measurement or a property supported by marked equal sides or other givens.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Link angle facts in a diagram
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: In triangle ABC, AB = AC and angle A = 36°. Extend BC beyond C to D. Find exterior angle ACD.
steps: The equal base angles B and C each equal (180° − 36°) ÷ 2 = 72°.
The exterior angle at C is 180° − 72° = 108°.

items.prompt: Two lines cross at O. One angle is 122°. The adjacent angle is split into 20° and x. Find x.
steps: The adjacent angle is 180° − 122° = 58°.
Remove the known 20° piece: x = 58° − 20° = 38°.

items.prompt: A, O, B form a straight line. Rays OC and OD lie on the same side in order A, C, D, B. AOC = 46° and DOB = 59°. Find COD.
steps: The three adjacent pieces fill a straight angle of 180°.

items.prompt: Three angles around O have ratio 2:3:4. Find the largest angle.
steps: Nine equal angle units make 360°, so one unit is 40°.
The largest occupies four units, or 160°; the other angles are 80° and 120°.

items.prompt: A triangle has angles 2x°, 3x° and 4x°. Find x and the largest angle.
steps: Nine equal units total 180°, so x = 180 ÷ 9 = 20.
The largest angle is 4x° = 80°; all three angles total 180°.

items.prompt: Give two different triangles whose angle at A is 50°. List the other angles and explain why A alone does not determine them.
steps: The other two angles need only total 130°.
Both pairs do so, so additional information is required to determine a unique pair.

weeks.objective: Use known triangle and quadrilateral properties without inserting extra lines.

connection.before: Use straight-line, point, opposite-angle and triangle totals in a sequence of deductions.
connection.after: Secondary geometry formalises proof; statistics compares several measures of centre.

Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: A square and a rectangle have four right angles. A parallelogram has opposite angles equal and adjacent angles totaling 180°. A rhombus is also a parallelogram, with all sides equal; do not infer its angles are right angles merely from equal side lengths.

In a composite figure, an already drawn diagonal or attached triangle divides a known angle into parts. If a rectangle corner is split into 32° and an unknown angle, the unknown is 58°. The triangle containing that 58° can then supply a further angle using its 180° total.

State which region owns each angle. At a shared vertex, adjacent interior angles may be added, while an exterior angle may need to be subtracted from a straight or full turn. Descriptions specify existing segments and the placement of attached shapes, so no extra construction is needed.

examples.prompt: ABCD is a rectangle with diagonal AC already drawn. Angle BAC = 34°. Find CAD and ACD.
steps: Diagonal AC lies inside the rectangle and divides its right-angle corner at A into BAC and CAD. Triangle ACD already has its right angle at D.
The rectangle corner at A is 90°, so CAD = 90° − 34° = 56°.
Triangle ACD has D = 90°, so ACD = 180° − 90° − 56° = 34°.

examples.prompt: ABCD is a parallelogram with angle A = 68°. Triangle BCE is attached outside along BC and has E = 42° and angle CBE = 53°. Find angle BCD and angle ECD, formed by BCE plus BCD.
steps: The parallelogram and attached triangle lie on opposite sides of BC. At C, the requested angle follows CE to CB to CD, combining their two interior angles.
Opposite parallelogram angles give BCD = 68°; in BCE, BCE = 180° − 42° − 53° = 85°.
The attached triangle is outside BC, so the angle from CE through CB to CD is 85° + 68° = 153°.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Angles in composite quadrilaterals
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A parallelogram has angle A = 73°. Find adjacent angle B and opposite angle C.
steps: Adjacent angles total 180°, so B = 180° − 73° = 107°.
Opposite angles are equal, so C = 73°.

items.prompt: A rectangle corner is split by an existing diagonal into 27° and x. Find x.
steps: The corner is a right angle, so both pieces total 90°.

items.prompt: A quadrilateral has interior angles 85°, 95°, 110° and x. Find x.
steps: The four interior angles of a quadrilateral total 360°.

items.prompt: ABCD is a square and diagonal AC is drawn. Find angle BAC.
steps: Triangle ABC has AB = BC and a right angle at B.
The two remaining equal angles total 90°, so each is 45°.

items.prompt: A rhombus has one angle of 58°. Find its other three interior angles.
steps: Opposite angles in a rhombus are equal.
Each adjacent angle is 180° − 58° = 122°.

items.prompt: A learner says every rhombus has four right angles because all four sides are equal. Explain the error.
items.answer: Equal sides do not force right angles.
steps: A rhombus can have angles 60°, 120°, 60°, 120°.
Opposite angles are equal and adjacent angles total 180°; right angles require an additional condition.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Angles in composite quadrilaterals
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: ABCD is a rectangle with diagonal BD. Angle ABD = 39°. Find DBC and BDC.
steps: The right angle at B gives DBC = 90° − 39° = 51°.
Triangle BCD has C = 90°, so BDC = 180° − 90° − 51° = 39°.

items.prompt: A parallelogram ABCD has angle B = 118°. Diagonal AC is drawn and angle BAC = 25°. Find CAD.
steps: Adjacent angles give angle A = 180° − 118° = 62°.
The diagonal splits A into BAC and CAD, so CAD = 62° − 25° = 37°.

items.prompt: In quadrilateral ABCD, diagonal AC is already drawn inside the figure. Triangle ABC has angles A = 40° and B = 75°; triangle ACD has angles A = 30° and D = 80°. Find the full angle BCD.
steps: Triangle ABC gives BCA = 180° − 40° − 75° = 65°; triangle ACD gives ACD = 70°.
The diagonal lies inside the quadrilateral, so BCD = 65° + 70° = 135°.

items.prompt: ABCD is a square. An isosceles triangle BCE with BE = CE is attached outside BC; its angle E is 40°. Find the angle from BA through BC to BE at B.
steps: The triangle base angle CBE is (180° − 40°) ÷ 2 = 70°.
It sits next to square angle ABC = 90°, so the specified combined angle is 160°.

items.prompt: ABCD is a trapezium with AB parallel to DC. Its interior angle A is 72°. Find interior angle D on the same leg AD.
steps: The angles on the same side of leg AD between parallel bases total 180°.

items.prompt: A proposed parallelogram has successive angles 80°, 100°, 90°, 90°. Can it be a parallelogram?
steps: Opposite angles would have to be equal.
Here 80° differs from its opposite 90°, so the parallelogram condition fails even though the total is 360°.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Angles in composite quadrilaterals
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: ABCD is a rectangle. Triangle ABE is attached outside AB, with E = 50° and A = 60° in the triangle. Find the combined angle from BC through BA to BE at B.
steps: Triangle ABE gives ABE = 180° − 50° − 60° = 70°.
This adjoins the 90° rectangle angle ABC, giving 160° along the stated route.

items.prompt: A parallelogram has adjacent interior angles in ratio 2:3. Find its two distinct angle sizes.
steps: The adjacent pair totals 180°, so five units make 180° and one unit is 36°.
Two units give 72° and three give 108°; opposite angles repeat these values.

items.prompt: ABCD is a quadrilateral with diagonal AC inside it. Triangle ABC has B = 90° and A = 28°. Triangle ACD has A = 42° and C = 63°. Find angles BAD and ADC.
steps: At A, the adjacent triangle angles sum to 28° + 42° = 70°.
Triangle ACD gives ADC = 180° − 42° − 63° = 75°.

items.prompt: A rectangle corner contains three non-overlapping angles of 18°, x and 47°. Find x and name the total used.
steps: The three pieces exactly fill one rectangle corner.

items.prompt: Two squares meet only at vertex O. Their right angles occupy adjacent non-overlapping sectors at O. Find the remaining angle around O.
steps: The two square angles together use 90° + 90° = 180°.
Subtract from the full 360° turn to get the remaining 180°.

items.prompt: A quadrilateral has three known angles totaling 250°. A learner says the fourth is 110°, but cannot name its type. Is the angle value justified?
items.answer: Yes; its type need not be known for this total.
steps: Every simple quadrilateral has interior-angle total 360°.
The fourth is 360° − 250° = 110°; the value alone does not identify a specific quadrilateral type.

weeks.title: Average as equal sharing
weeks.objective: Connect average, total and number of values through a redistribution model.

connection.before: Use known triangle and quadrilateral properties without inserting extra lines.
connection.after: Secondary geometry formalises proof; statistics compares several measures of centre.

days: Build or sketch a model for average as equal sharing; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: Place counters in piles matching the data: 4, 6 and 8. Move counters from the tallest pile to the shortest until all three piles contain 6. The total remains 18, so the average is the equal-share amount 18 ÷ 3 = 6. Individual values need not equal the average.

The three linked quantities are total = average × number of values, average = total ÷ number of values, and number of values = total ÷ average when the average is nonzero. Count every included value, including zero. Use labels to decide whether the data are daily totals, lengths, scores or something else.

An average may be fractional even when every original value is a whole-number count. It summarizes equal sharing and does not claim that a particular day had a fractional count. The average must lie between the least and greatest values, and multiplying it by the count must recover the total.

examples.prompt: Four boxes hold 5, 7, 8 and 12 counters. Find the average counters per box.
steps: Represent the four box counts as piles of 5, 7, 8 and 12 counters. Redistributing between the four piles preserves the combined count.
The total is 5 + 7 + 8 + 12 = 32.
Share this total equally among 4 values: 32 ÷ 4 = 8.

examples.prompt: Six equal-length practice sessions average 14 points each. Find the total points.
steps: Represent the average with six equal bars of fourteen points. Their combined length matches the actual session total even if individual scores differ.
Multiply the number of sessions by the average share: 6 × 14 = 84 points in all.
Check by equal sharing: 84 ÷ 6 = 14 points per session, matching the stated average.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Average as equal sharing
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Find the average of 6, 10 and 14.
steps: The total is 6 + 10 + 14 = 30.
Share this total equally among 3 values: 30 ÷ 3 = 10.

items.prompt: Four measured lengths are 12, 15, 18 and 19 cm. Find their average in cm.
steps: The total is 12 + 15 + 18 + 19 = 64.
Share this total equally among 4 values: 64 ÷ 4 = 16.

items.prompt: Sales on five days are 2, 4, 0, 6 and 8 items. Find average daily sales.
steps: The total is 2 + 4 + 0 + 6 + 8 = 20.
Share this total equally among 5 values: 20 ÷ 5 = 4.

items.prompt: Five boxes average 9 marbles each. Find the total number of marbles.
steps: The total can be rebuilt from five equal average shares.
5 × 9 = 45, even if actual boxes differ.

items.prompt: A total of 72 points is recorded over 8 rounds. Find the average.
steps: The count is eight rounds and the total is 72.
Divide 72 by 8 to equalize the scores: 9.

items.prompt: A pupil omits a zero when averaging 0, 4, 8 and 12. Explain the correct divisor and answer.
steps: There are four observations, including the zero.
Their total is 24; 24 ÷ 4 = 6, not 24 ÷ 3.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Average as equal sharing
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Seven daily totals are 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15. Find their average.
steps: Share this total equally among 7 values: 63 ÷ 7 = 9.

items.prompt: Three bottles hold 0.6 L, 0.9 L and 1.2 L. Find the average volume in L.
steps: Share this total equally among 3 values: 2.7 ÷ 3 = 0.9.

items.prompt: Four game scores average 18. Explain why this does not mean every score was 18.
items.answer: Different scores can have the same total 72.
steps: For example, 15, 17, 19 and 21 sum to 72.
Sharing 72 over four scores gives 18 although none equals 18.

items.prompt: Can 20 be the average of 7, 9, 11 and 13? Explain without calculating their exact average.
steps: Every value is at most 13.
An equal-share average cannot exceed the largest value, so 20 is impossible.

items.prompt: A total of 96 seeds is shared across trays with average 12 per tray. How many trays are there?
steps: Each average share corresponds to one tray.
96 ÷ 12 = 8; 8 × 12 returns the total.

items.prompt: Three piles contain 2, 8 and 11 counters. How many should be moved from the largest pile to the smallest so all three can eventually become equal? Give a complete redistribution.
items.answer: Move 4 from the 11-pile to the 2-pile, then 1 from the 8-pile to that pile.
steps: The total is 21, so the target is 7 per pile.
After the moves the piles become 7, 7, 7; other moves with the same final piles are valid.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Average as equal sharing
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A reader completes 9, 12, 15, 16 and 18 pages on five days. Find average pages per day.
steps: Share this total equally among 5 values: 70 ÷ 5 = 14.

items.prompt: Six bottles contain 4.2 L altogether. Find the average volume per bottle in mL.
steps: Convert the total to 4200 mL.
Divide by six bottles: 4200 ÷ 6 = 700 mL.

items.prompt: Two classes each have 5 measurement records. One class total is 70 cm and the other total is 90 cm. Find the average of all ten measurements.
steps: Combine the totals: 70 + 90 = 160 cm.
Combine the counts: 5 + 5 = 10; average = 160 ÷ 10 = 16 cm.

items.prompt: Two days have 5 and 8 visitors. Explain whether an average of 6.5 visitors is valid.
steps: The combined count is 13 over two days, so 13 ÷ 2 = 6.5.
This is an equal-share summary, not a claim that half a person visited on a day.

items.prompt: Create four whole-number scores with average 8 and at least two different scores.
steps: Their sum must be 4 × 8 = 32.
These four sum to 32 and are not all equal; other sets meeting both conditions are valid.

items.prompt: Five lengths have average 14 cm. Every length increases by 2 cm. Find the new average.
steps: The total rises by 5 × 2 = 10 cm.
Sharing that increase across five values raises the average by 2 cm, from 14 to 16.

weeks.title: Recover missing data and combined averages
weeks.objective: Reconstruct a total before finding a missing value or joining groups.

connection.before: Connect average, total and number of values through a redistribution model.
connection.after: Secondary geometry formalises proof; statistics compares several measures of centre.

days: Build or sketch a model for recover missing data and combined averages; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: An average and a count together tell us the exact total. If four scores average 15, they total 60. If three known scores total 41, the missing score is 60 − 41 = 19. A bar of four average shares is a model for the total, not a claim that the original four scores were equal.

Adding or removing a value changes both the total and the count. Rebuild the old total, apply the change, then divide by the new count. When two groups are joined, add their totals and their counts. Averaging the two group averages only works automatically when the group counts are equal.

Check reconstructed data against any limits in the question. A missing score of 27 is impossible on a twenty-point task, even if it follows from the supplied average. For open data sets, many answers may fit the same total; state a valid example and verify the total and count.

examples.prompt: Four scores average 18. Three scores are 12, 19 and 20. Find the fourth.
steps: Draw four equal average bars of eighteen to represent the required total, then reserve portions for the three known scores.
The required total is 18 × 4 = 72.
The known values total 51; subtract to find the missing value 72 − 51 = 21.

examples.prompt: Three trays average 8 seeds and five other trays average 12 seeds. Find the average across all eight trays.
steps: The first group contains three eight-seed average shares; the second contains five twelve-seed average shares. Count all eight trays in the final sharing.
The two totals are 3 × 8 = 24 and 5 × 12 = 60, giving 84 seeds.
There are eight trays, so the combined average is 84 ÷ 8 = 10.5.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Recover missing data and combined averages
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Five values average 10. Four are 6, 8, 11 and 13. Find the fifth.
steps: The required total is 10 × 5 = 50.
The known values total 38; subtract to find the missing value 50 − 38 = 12.

items.prompt: Three lengths average 16 cm. Two are 13 cm and 18 cm. Find the missing length in cm.
steps: The required total is 16 × 3 = 48.
The known values total 31; subtract to find the missing value 48 − 31 = 17.

items.prompt: Four days average 25 visitors. The first three days have 18, 22 and 31. Find the fourth day count.
steps: The required total is 25 × 4 = 100.
The known values total 71; subtract to find the missing value 100 − 71 = 29.

items.prompt: Six scores average 9. A seventh score is 16. Find the new average.
steps: The original total is 6 × 9 = 54; add 16 to get 70.
Divide by the new count seven: 70 ÷ 7 = 10.

items.prompt: Five numbers average 14. Remove a number equal to 18. Find the average of the four remaining.
steps: The original total is 70, leaving 70 − 18 = 52.

items.prompt: Two groups have averages 10 and 20. Why is 15 not always their combined average?
steps: For one value of 10 and three values of 20, the total is 70 over four values.
The combined average is 17.5; each group total must be weighted by its count.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Recover missing data and combined averages
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Six readings average 7. Five readings are 3, 4, 6, 8 and 9. Find the sixth.
steps: The required total is 7 × 6 = 42.
The known values total 30; subtract to find the missing value 42 − 30 = 12.

items.prompt: Two boxes average 15 beads and four boxes average 9 beads. Find the average over all six.
steps: The totals are 2 × 15 = 30 and 4 × 9 = 36.
The combined total 66 divided by six is 11.

items.prompt: Four values average 12. One value is corrected from 9 to 17. Find the corrected average.
steps: The correction adds 8 to the total of 48, making 56.
56 ÷ 4 = 14; the count does not change.

items.prompt: Three scores on 20-point tasks average 18. Two scores are 10 and 16. Is the stated average possible?
steps: The required total is 3 × 18 = 54.
The missing score would be 54 − 26 = 28, above the maximum 20.

items.prompt: Four bags average 11 kg. Two more bags each weigh 8 kg. Find the new average.
steps: The original total is 44 kg; the added bags contribute 16 kg.
60 kg shared over six bags gives 10 kg.

items.prompt: A set of five values averages 20. A sixth value is added and the average stays 20. Find the added value.
steps: The old total is 100 and the new total must be 6 × 20 = 120.
The added value is 120 − 100 = 20.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Recover missing data and combined averages
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A reader wants to average 16 pages over five days. The first four days total 61 pages. How many pages are needed on day five?
steps: The target total is 5 × 16 = 80 pages.
Subtract the completed 61 pages to get 19.

items.prompt: Four club sessions average 24 participants. A fifth session has 34. Find the new average attendance.
steps: The first four total 96 attendances.
Add 34 to get 130 and divide by five sessions: 26.

items.prompt: Five cartons average 18 bottles. One carton of 10 is removed and another of 25 is added. Find the new average across five cartons.
steps: The total changes from 90 to 90 − 10 + 25 = 105.
The carton count remains five, so average = 105 ÷ 5 = 21.

items.prompt: Two known values are 7 and 13. Add two nonnegative whole numbers to make the average of all four equal 12. Give two possible pairs.
steps: The required total is 48 and the known sum is 20, so the two additions must total 28.
Both pairs total 28; any two nonnegative whole numbers with that sum work.

items.prompt: Three lengths average 12 cm, and two more lengths average 17 cm. A learner reports an overall average of 14.5 cm. Correct it.
steps: The combined total is 3 × 12 + 2 × 17 = 70 cm.
There are five lengths; 70 ÷ 5 = 14 cm, because the group sizes are unequal.

items.prompt: Four scores average 15. The largest score, 21, is removed. What must the average of the rest be, and is the largest-score detail needed?
items.answer: 13; the removed value and count are sufficient.
steps: The original total is 60, leaving 39 after removing 21.
There are three scores left, so the average is 13; no ordering information is needed for this calculation.

weeks.title: Choose the conserved total
weeks.objective: Choose an angle total or a data total and justify which quantities belong to it.

connection.before: Reconstruct a total before finding a missing value or joining groups.
connection.after: Secondary geometry formalises proof; statistics compares several measures of centre.

days: Build or sketch a model for choose the conserved total; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: Geometry and averages both use totals, but their totals come from different structures. Three triangle angles total 180° because they form one triangle. Five scores averaging 12 total 60 because five equal average shares would hold the same sum. Label the structure before doing subtraction.

A composite problem can mix totals without mixing their meanings. The four interior angles of a quadrilateral total 360°, so their average is 90°. This does not make every quadrilateral angle a right angle. Likewise, a triangle angle average of 60° does not prove the triangle is equilateral.

When a number is missing, first find the appropriate complete total, then remove the known contributions. Check both the arithmetic and the conditions: an angle must fit the stated figure, and a score must fit any given range. A true average statement may leave individual values undetermined.

examples.prompt: A quadrilateral has angles 80°, 95°, 105° and x. Find x and the average of its four angles.
steps: The four angles belong to one quadrilateral, so use its fixed 360° interior-angle total before finding the missing angle or the average.
The missing angle is 360° − 80° − 95° − 105° = 80°.
All four angles total 360°, so their average is 360° ÷ 4 = 90°.

examples.prompt: Five angle measurements average 42°. Four are 30°, 35°, 45° and 50°. Find the fifth; these are separate measurements, not one polygon.
steps: These five angles are separate data readings. Their total comes from five copies of the stated 42° average, not from a polygon rule.
The data total is 5 × 42° = 210°, not a polygon total.
The known sum is 160°, so the missing measurement is 50°.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Choose the conserved total
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Find the average size of the three interior angles of any triangle.
steps: Every triangle has interior-angle total 180°.
Divide by three angles: 180° ÷ 3 = 60°.

items.prompt: Does an average interior angle of 90° prove a quadrilateral is a rectangle? Explain with angle values.
steps: Those angles total 360°, giving average 90°.
They are not all right angles, so the average alone cannot establish a rectangle.

items.prompt: A triangle has one angle 40° and its other two angles are equal. Find all angles and their average.
steps: The equal angles share 180° − 40° = 140°, so each is 70°.
The total divided by three gives 60°, different from each of two angle sizes.

items.prompt: Four measured angles, unrelated to one figure, are 20°, 40°, 60° and 100°. Find their average in degrees.
steps: Share this total equally among 4 values: 220 ÷ 4 = 55.

items.prompt: Four angles around a point are all equal. Find each and explain why an average now determines every angle.
steps: The full turn of 360° is divided into four equal parts.
The equality condition makes each angle equal to the average 360° ÷ 4 = 90°.

items.prompt: A learner adds 180 to data 8, 10 and 12 before finding an average. Explain the mistake and find the average.
steps: The data total is 8 + 10 + 12 = 30; no triangle is stated.
180° is a geometry total, not an extra data value; divide 30 by 3.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Choose the conserved total
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Five scores average 16. One score is 24. Find the average of the other four.
steps: The full total is 5 × 16 = 80.
Remove 24 to get 56, then divide by four.

items.prompt: A parallelogram has an angle of 64°. Find the average of that angle and an adjacent angle.
steps: The adjacent angle is 180° − 64° = 116°.
Their total is 180° across two angles, so their average is 90°.

items.prompt: Two triangles have angles (30°, 60°, 90°) and (50°, 60°, 70°). Find the average of all six angles.
steps: The two triangle totals together are 360°.
Divide by six measured angles to get 60°.

items.prompt: A straight angle is split into three parts. Two are 45° and 65°. Find the third part and average part size.
steps: The third part is 180° − 45° − 65° = 70°.
All three parts average 180° ÷ 3 = 60°.

items.prompt: Four nonnegative scores average 6. Can one score be 30? Explain.
steps: The total of all four is only 4 × 6 = 24.
A single score of 30 would force the others to sum to −6, impossible for nonnegative scores.

items.prompt: Angles in one triangle are listed as 50°, 60° and 80°. A learner finds average 190/3 degrees. What should be corrected first?
items.answer: The listed angles cannot form a triangle.
steps: Their sum is 190°, not 180°.
The data average is arithmetically possible, but the geometric claim fails before a triangle conclusion can be made.

items.prompt: A club records five weekly attendances averaging 28. The first two weeks total 49. Find the average for the last three weeks.
steps: The complete total is 5 × 28 = 140.
The last three total 140 − 49 = 91; 91 ÷ 3 = 30⅓.

items.prompt: In a rectangle, an existing diagonal splits one corner into two angles. Their difference is 18°. Find the two angles.
steps: Their total is 90°; remove the excess 18° to leave 72° for two equal smaller parts.
The smaller is 36°, and the larger is 54°; both sum and difference check.

items.prompt: A triangle has angles in ratio 3:4:5. Find the average of the smallest and largest angles.
steps: Twelve units make 180°, so the angles are 45°, 60° and 75°.
The smallest and largest sum to 120°; divide by two to obtain 60°.

items.prompt: Four trial times average 18 seconds. A fifth trial raises the average to 20 seconds. Find its time.
steps: The old total is 72 seconds and the new total is 100 seconds.
The added trial is the difference: 100 − 72 = 28 seconds.

items.prompt: Can two groups of three triangle angles have different averages? Explain under valid Euclidean triangle conditions.
steps: Each group contains exactly the three interior angles of one triangle, totalling 180°.
Dividing either total by three gives the same average, regardless of shape.

items.prompt: Construct four angles of a valid parallelogram whose average is 90° but none is 90°.
steps: Opposite angles are equal and adjacent angles total 180°.
The full total is 360° and its average is 90°; any non-right positive supplementary pair repeated works.

explanation: A planning problem can contain several totals. Suppose 72 craft sheets are split between two rooms in ratio 5:4. The nine ratio units describe all sheets, while a later price per packet describes cost. Solve the allocation first: each unit is eight sheets, giving 40 and 32.

Choose an equation when the unknown repeats in identical groups. If six packets and seven loose sheets contain 61 sheets, let x be sheets per packet and write 6x + 7 = 61. A bar model removes the seven loose sheets and splits the remaining 54 into six equal packet bars.

A feasible plan must meet every stated condition, including whole objects, leftovers and recipients. After calculating a candidate, recombine its shares, simplify the ratio and check packaging. If the total is incompatible with exact whole-number shares, explain the conflict rather than rounding the shares silently.

examples.prompt: A club divides 96 sheets between painting and folding in ratio 5:3. Folding uses its sheets in groups of 4. How many groups can it supply?
steps: The complete allocation has eight equal ratio units: five for painting and three for folding. The four-sheet group size applies only after finding folding sheets.
Eight ratio units make 96 sheets, so folding receives 3 × 12 = 36.
36 ÷ 4 = 9 complete groups; painting receives 60 and the total checks.

examples.prompt: Five identical packets and 8 loose pencils contain 68 pencils. The packets are shared between two tables in ratio 2:3. How many packet pencils go to the second table?
steps: The eight loose pencils sit outside the five equal packet bars. The second table receives three of those five whole packets.
Let x be pencils per packet: 5x + 8 = 68, so x = 12.
The second table receives three packets, giving 3 × 12 = 36 pencils; the loose eight are separate.

worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A club splits 66 badges between two teams in ratio 4:7. How many go to the smaller team?
steps: The bar contains 11 equal units, so one unit is 66 ÷ 11 = 6.
The requested 4 units give 24; all parts together recover 66.

items.prompt: A:B:C = 2:3:4 describes a 108-card allocation. Find all three shares.
steps: The nine units give one unit as 108 ÷ 9 = 12.
Multiply 12 by 2, 3 and 4; the three counts sum to 108.

items.prompt: A supply rule is 4x + 6 = 54, where x is counters per bag. Find x.
steps: Undo the addition of 6: 4x = 48.
Divide by 4 to get x = 12; substitution gives 4 × 12 + 6 = 54.

items.prompt: A plan needs 6 tables with 8 scissors each. Packs contain 12 scissors. Find the number of packs needed with no leftovers.
steps: The required total is 6 × 8 = 48 scissors.
48 ÷ 12 = 4 packs, and four packs supply exactly the total.

items.prompt: A total of 50 tokens must be shared exactly in ratio 3:4 using whole tokens. Explain whether the plan is feasible.
steps: There are seven common ratio units.
50 is not divisible by seven, so exact shares would require fractional tokens.

items.prompt: A learner allocates 84 cards in ratio 2:5 as 24 and 60. Check both conditions.
steps: 24 + 60 = 84 preserves the total.
24:60 simplifies to 2:5 by dividing both terms by 12.

worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A craft kit has x beads in each of 3 bags and 5 loose beads. Write its total, then evaluate for x = 9.
steps: Three equal bags contribute 3x and the loose beads add 5.
Substitute 9 to obtain 27 + 5 = 32.

items.prompt: Two groups receive cards in ratio 3:8. The larger receives 64 cards. Find the whole allocation.
steps: Eight units equal 64, so one unit is 8 cards.
The smaller receives 24; total = 24 + 64 = 88.

items.prompt: A table needs 18 red and 24 blue beads. Another table needs the same colour ratio but 35 beads total. Find its counts.
steps: The original ratio simplifies to 3:4, seven units in all.
Each new unit is 35 ÷ 7 = 5; the new counts are 15 and 20.

items.prompt: Three activity stations use 24, 30 and 42 stickers. Find the average sticker use per station.
steps: The combined use is 24 + 30 + 42 = 96.
Divide by three stations: 96 ÷ 3 = 32.

items.prompt: Four identical boxes hold 52 crayons total. A fifth identical box is added. Find the new total.
steps: Each box holds 52 ÷ 4 = 13 crayons.
Five boxes hold 5 × 13 = 65.

items.prompt: A club has 90 sheets. It sets aside 18 and splits the rest equally between 6 tables. Find each table share.
steps: The amount available for tables is 90 − 18 = 72 sheets.
Divide 72 by six tables to get 12 each.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Plan a club supply allocation
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A club allocates 120 cards in ratio drawing:writing = 3:2. Drawing gives 12 cards to writing. Find the final ratio.
steps: The initial shares are 72 and 48.
After transfer they are 60 and 60, so the final ratio is 1:1.

items.prompt: A plan allocates 2 red and 3 blue counters per player. There are 12 players and 75 counters available. How many counters remain if the colour supply is sufficient?
steps: Each player needs five counters, so twelve need 60.
75 − 60 = 15 remain; colour availability is explicitly assumed.

items.prompt: Three stations share 84 tokens in ratio 2:3:7. The largest station needs 45 tokens. Does its share suffice?
steps: One unit is 84 ÷ 12 = 7 tokens.
The largest share is 7 × 7 = 49; compare it with the need of 45.

items.prompt: A committee buys 5 packs containing x sheets each. After using 17 sheets, 43 remain. Find x and verify.
steps: The initial total is 17 + 43 = 60, so 5x = 60.
x = 12; five packs give 60 and removing 17 leaves 43.

items.prompt: Design a whole-card allocation below 100 in ratio 4:5 with both groups receiving at least 20 cards. Give one plan.
items.answer: For example, 45 cards split as 20 and 25
steps: Five cards per ratio unit gives shares 4 × 5 and 5 × 5.
Both meet the minimum and their total 45 is below 100; larger valid unit sizes are possible.

items.prompt: The only data given are A:B = 2:7 and A receives 10 fewer than B. Can this describe whole counters?
steps: Five excess units make 10 counters, so one unit is 2.
The counts are 4 and 14, with ratio 2:7 and difference 10.

weeks.title: Build and compare a simple budget
weeks.objective: Use expressions, equations and ratio shares to test a cost plan.

connection.before: Choose bars or equations to connect ratio allocations with a fixed total.
connection.after: Begin S1 by revisiting these models and extending the number system beyond positive quantities.

days: Build or sketch a model for build and compare a simple budget; explain what each unit represents.
Read the two examples and connect each line to the model.
Use worksheet A to make the relationship visible and discuss one error.
Use worksheet B to compare methods; check by reversing the calculation.
Choose worksheet C applications and explain how the result meets the givens.
explanation: A budget model starts by defining what varies and what is fixed. If each kit costs $4 and transport costs $12 once, the total for n kits is 4n + 12. The twelve dollars is not charged for each kit. Evaluate the expression only after deciding how many kits the plan needs.

Compare plans at the same number of kits and include every stated fixed charge. For a budget cap, a candidate must leave a nonnegative remainder. A whole-number kit count matters: a quotient between whole numbers may mean only the lower complete count is affordable.

Ratio allocations describe shares of the budget, whereas average spending describes a total divided by a count. Write the units alongside the numbers. An average cost per participant can include shared fixed costs, so it may differ from the stated price of one individual item.

examples.prompt: A workshop buys 18 kits at $3 each and pays one $16 delivery fee. Find total cost and money left from $80.
steps: Draw eighteen equal $3 kit costs and one separate $16 delivery block. The $80 budget must cover their combined value.
The kits cost 18 × 3 = $54; add the one fixed $16 fee to get $70.
Subtract $70 from the $80 budget, leaving $10.

examples.prompt: A $144 budget is split materials:refreshments = 5:3. Materials kits cost $6 each. How many kits can the materials share buy?
steps: Split the full $144 bar into eight units, with five units assigned to materials. Only that five-unit share can pay for the $6 kits.
Eight ratio units give $18 per unit; materials receive 5 × 18 = $90.
$90 ÷ $6 per kit = 15 kits, using the materials share exactly.

worksheets.title: Models and meaning: Build and compare a simple budget
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Plan A costs 5x + 9 dollars for x tickets. Find the cost of 8 tickets.
steps: Replace each x by 8; 5x means 5 × 8 = 40.
Add 9 to get 49; multiply before adding or subtracting.

items.prompt: A $75 budget pays a fixed $15 fee plus $4 per kit. Find the greatest whole number of kits affordable.
steps: After the fixed fee, $60 remains for kits.

items.prompt: Write a cost expression for n $7 notebooks and one $5 box.
steps: The notebooks contribute n groups of $7.
The box adds $5 once, after the notebook cost.

items.prompt: A budget splits travel:food = 2:5. Travel receives $36. Find the total budget.
steps: Two units equal $36, so one unit is $18.
Seven total units give 7 × 18 = $126.

items.prompt: Five identical posters and a $4 tube cost $39. Find one poster price.
steps: Remove the fixed tube cost: 39 − 4 = $35.
Divide among five equal poster prices: 35 ÷ 5 = $7.

items.prompt: A learner models 6 tickets at $x each plus one $8 fee as 14x. Correct the model.
steps: Only six quantities have the unknown price x.
The fee is a fixed eight dollars, not eight more tickets.

worksheets.title: Connections and methods: Build and compare a simple budget
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: Plan A costs 4n + 20 dollars and plan B costs 5n + 8 dollars. Compare their costs for n = 10.
items.answer: A costs $60; B costs $58, so B is $2 cheaper.
steps: Substitute 10 into A: 40 + 20 = 60.
Substitute 10 into B: 50 + 8 = 58; compare final totals.

items.prompt: The plans 4n + 20 and 5n + 8 both cost $68 when n = 12. Verify this claim.
A group spends $96 across 8 participants. Find the average spending per participant.
steps: The full $96 is the total to be shared for the summary.
Divide by eight participants: 96 ÷ 8 = $12.

items.prompt: Three sessions cost $28, $34 and $40. A fourth brings the average to $35. Find its cost.
steps: Four sessions need a total of 4 × 35 = $140.
The known total is 102; the missing cost is 140 − 102 = $38.

items.prompt: A $90 budget has supplies:food:prizes = 4:3:2. Find the prize share and unused money if prizes cost $17.
steps: Nine units mean $10 per unit, so prizes receive $20.
Subtract actual prize spending: 20 − 17 = $3.

items.prompt: A $50 budget pays $7 per box plus a $6 fee. Why is buying 7 boxes not feasible?
items.answer: The bill would be $55, which is $5 over budget.
steps: Seven boxes cost 7 × 7 = $49.
The fixed fee makes the total 49 + 6 = $55; only six boxes fit the cap.

worksheets.title: Applications and checks: Build and compare a simple budget
worksheets.directions: Show a labelled bar, calculation or explanation. State units and check that your answer fits every given condition.

items.prompt: A class buys 24 pencils at 50 cents each and 6 erasers at $1 each. Find total cost in dollars.
steps: Twenty-four pencils cost 1200 cents = $12.
Six erasers cost $6, making total $18.

items.prompt: Two groups share a $108 bill in ratio 5:4. The first group has 9 people who pay equally. Find their payment per person.
items.answer: $20/3, or $6⅔, per person before any cash-rounding rule
steps: The first group share is 5/9 × 108 = $60.
Divide its $60 equally among 9 people: 60/9 = 20/3 dollars; no cent-rounding rule was supplied.

items.prompt: A supplier offers packs of 8 markers for $12. A club needs 30 markers and must buy whole packs. Find packs, cost and spare markers.
steps: Three packs provide only 24, so four are required and provide 32.
Four packs cost 4 × 12 = $48, with 32 − 30 = 2 spare.

items.prompt: A club has $100. After a $16 fee it buys 12 identical kits and has $12 left. Find the price of one kit.
steps: Kit spending is 100 − 16 − 12 = $72.
Divide by 12 kits to obtain $6; 16 + 72 + 12 = 100 checks the budget.

items.prompt: Choose a whole-number kit count of at least 10 for a plan costing 3n + 14 dollars, with a $50 cap. Give all possible counts.
steps: The cap leaves 50 − 14 = $36 for $3 kits, allowing at most 12.
Combining n ≥ 10 with n ≤ 12 gives the three whole-number choices.

items.prompt: A quoted average of $8 for 15 people excludes a fixed $30 venue fee. Find the average per person after including the fee.
steps: The quoted total is 15 × 8 = $120; add $30 to get $150.
Divide the complete total by 15: 150 ÷ 15 = $10.
